嘉靖癸卯秋八月，應天府鄉試。府臣先期疏請考試官，上以命侍讀臣察、中允臣如霖。至，則同考爲學正臣琮、臣廷琮，教諭臣彥錦、臣密、臣繼英、臣鑰、臣仲玉、臣薇；監試爲御史臣存誠、臣驗。提調事則屬之府丞臣學益，而府尹臣瀚繼至，亦與有勞焉。

translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn in the guimao year of Jiajing [1543], Yingtian Prefecture held its Provincial Examination. Before the appointed date, the prefectural officials submitted a memorial requesting Examiners. His Majesty appointed Reader Cha and Assistant to the Heir Apparent Rulin. Upon their arrival, the Associate Examiners were the Confucian School Instructors Cong and Tingcong, and the County School Instructors Yanjin, Mi, Jiying, Yue, Zhongyu, and Wei. The Censors Cuncheng and Yan supervised the examination. The duties of Proctor were entrusted to Vice Prefect Xueyi. Prefect Han subsequently arrived and also contributed to the work.

At that time, those presenting themselves for examination—from the six halls and the various offices, together with those selected by Education-Intendant Censor Yang Yi—numbered more than 4,500 in all. Following established practice, they were examined in three sessions. Their outstanding candidates were assessed, and 135 men were selected. text:
獻臣竊惟今
南畿於古為吳楚之境當周之中
世二國號稱多士其疆域雖介
在一隅而文物之盛則已抗衡
中夏由漢以來作者代興所謂
東南之美不徒竹箭而已者乃
自古記之矣我
===

宮府兵衛之設於南者如故

獻。臣竊惟，今南畿於古為吳楚之境。當周之中世，二國號稱多士，其疆域雖介在一隅，而文物之盛則已抗衡中夏。由漢以來，作者代興，所謂「東南之美，不徒竹箭而已」者，乃自古記之矣。
我高皇帝創業建都金陵，盡江淮之地，東濱於海，畫為畿甸。文皇帝紹統，定鼎於北，而宮府兵衛之設於南者如故。兩都竝峙，比周豐鎬。一時佐命元勲，大抵出於豐沛徐揚間。至
translation_en:
…to present to the throne. Your servant humbly reflects that the present Southern Metropolitan Region lay in antiquity within the territories of Wu and Chu. In the middle period of the Zhou dynasty, these two states were renowned for their many worthy men. Although their territories occupied only one corner of the realm, their flourishing cultural accomplishments already rivaled those of the Central States. From the Han onward, distinguished writers arose in every generation. Thus the saying that “the finest products of the southeast are not merely bamboo arrow-shafts” has been recorded since antiquity.
Our Emperor Gao founded the dynasty and established his capital at Jinling. He designated the entire territory of the Jiang and Huai rivers, extending eastward to the sea, as the metropolitan domain. Emperor Wen succeeded to the imperial line and established the seat of rule in the north, while the palaces, government offices, troops, and guards established in the south remained as before. The two capitals stood side by side, comparable to Feng and Hao under the Zhou. The great founding statesmen who assisted in establishing the dynasty came for the most part from the areas of Feng, Pei, Xu, and Yang. As for…

百七十餘年
聖化涵濡雖場屋程試之文亦月異
歲改有獨盛於天下者臣頊承
之乃獲寓目焉以極夫瑰瑋閎
肆之觀詎非幸歟雖然臣竊有
慮焉
國家以經術取士其習甚正洪武
punctuated:
於館閣侍從之臣，亦南産居多，相與作為文章，以黼黻治功。其播於絲綸、著於賦詠，颯颯乎典謨雅頌之遺矣。人材之盛，蓋與周人所稱「思皇多士，生此王國」者寔相媲美，彼區區偏方之習不論也。
百七十餘年，聖化涵濡，雖場屋程試之文，亦月異歲改，有獨盛於天下者。臣頃承乏，乃獲寓目焉，以極夫瑰瑋閎肆之觀，詎非幸歟？雖然，臣竊有慮焉。國家以經術取士，其習甚正。洪武
translation_en:
…as for the court attendants serving in the literary academies, most likewise were natives of the south. Together they composed writings that adorned the achievements of government. Disseminated in imperial pronouncements and expressed in rhapsodies and verse, these writings stirred with the surviving spirit of the Canonical Documents and Counsels and the Odes and Hymns. The abundance of talent truly rivaled what the men of Zhou celebrated in the words, “How splendid the many worthy men, born in this royal kingdom!” The narrow conventions of a peripheral region scarcely merit discussion by comparison.
For more than a hundred and seventy years, the civilizing influence of our sage rulers has permeated all. Even the compositions submitted for assessment in the examination halls have changed month by month and year by year, attaining a distinction unrivaled throughout the realm. Recently, your servant was called upon, for want of someone more capable, to serve in this office, and thus gained the opportunity to read them and behold to the full their marvelous richness, breadth, and exuberance. Was this not a blessing? Nevertheless, your servant privately harbors a concern. The state selects its scholars through learning in the Classics, and this practice is most correct. During the Hongwu …

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
永樂間士爲文簡而暢質而□
如大匠制器不事琱琢而渾樸
之意獨存其見於猷爲以經世
宰物者亦皆敦厚博大稱其所
言文之實用於是乎在今海内
之文非不富且麗矣顧其間或
衒奇務博力去陳言而意不免
===
於晦僻甚者離棄傳註踰越繩
檢以浮豔相高而不槩於理及
其出而致用雖議論藻飾克蔚
可觀而夷考其實則視前輩或
劣焉昔之君子論文以慕遠忽
近貴華賤實爲世道慮眞知言
哉

於晦僻甚者離棄傳註踰越繩
檢以浮豔相高而不槩於理及
其出而致用雖議論藻飾克蔚
可觀而夷考其實則視前輩或
劣焉昔之君子論文以慕遠忽
近貴華賤實爲世道慮眞知言
哉
punctuated: 永樂間，士爲文簡而暢，質而□，如大匠制器，不事琱琢，而渾樸之意獨存。其見於猷爲，以經世宰物者，亦皆敦厚博大，稱其所言。文之實用，於是乎在。今海内之文，非不富且麗矣，顧其間或衒奇務博，力去陳言，而意不免於晦僻。甚者離棄傳註，踰越繩檢，以浮豔相高，而不槩於理。及其出而致用，雖議論藻飾，克蔚可觀，而夷考其實，則視前輩或劣焉。昔之君子論文，以慕遠忽近、貴華賤實爲世道慮，眞知言哉！
translation_en:
…and during the Yongle reign, scholars wrote with brevity and fluency, with plainness and [illegible], like master craftsmen making vessels: they did not concern themselves with carving and embellishment, yet preserved an unadorned integrity. What they manifested in their plans and actions, ordering the world and governing its affairs, was likewise substantial and magnanimous, commensurate with their words. Herein lay the practical utility of writing.

Writing throughout the realm today is certainly rich and elegant. Yet some writers flaunt novelty and strive to display broad learning, straining to discard familiar expressions, while their meaning inevitably becomes obscure and abstruse. The worst abandon the authoritative commentaries, transgress established bounds, and vie with one another in superficial ornament, without conforming to principle. When they enter public service and put their learning to use, their arguments may be embellished and splendid to behold; but a dispassionate examination of their actual achievements finds them sometimes inferior to their predecessors. When gentlemen of old discussed writing, they worried about the condition of the world because writers admired the remote and neglected the near, prized ornament and slighted substance. How truly they understood the matter!

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聖天子勵精圖治稽古右文而尤屬
意選舉屢
詔所司以端士習正文體爲先務
識者知淳風之回而斯文之復
於古也臣等被
命夙夜兢惕惟不得人以仰副
聖心是懼用敢竭其愚以從事今茲
===
所取惟理明詞達而晦僻浮豔
如前所云者弗與焉蓋將示之
意嚮使知夫文之實用在此不
在彼也庶其有益乎抑聞昔王
之制治也以質文相變質勝則
濟之以文文勝則矯之以質
南畿之文盛矣臣懼其質之未至

所取惟理明詞達而晦僻浮豔
如前所云者弗與焉蓋將示之
意嚮使知夫文之實用在此不
在彼也庶其有益乎抑聞昔王
之制治也以質文相變質勝則
濟之以文文勝則矯之以質
南畿之文盛矣臣懼其質之未至
punctuated:
聖天子勵精圖治，稽古右文，而尤屬意選舉，屢詔所司以端士習、正文體爲先務。識者知淳風之回，而斯文之復於古也。臣等被命，夙夜兢惕，惟不得人以仰副聖心是懼，用敢竭其愚以從事。今茲所取，惟理明詞達，而晦僻浮豔如前所云者弗與焉。蓋將示之意嚮，使知夫文之實用在此不在彼也。庶其有益乎！
抑聞昔王之制治也，以質文相變：質勝則濟之以文，文勝則矯之以質。南畿之文盛矣，臣懼其質之未至
translation_en:
The sagely Son of Heaven devotes himself diligently to good government, examines antiquity, and esteems literary culture. He pays particular attention to the selection of men for office, repeatedly ordering the responsible officials to make rectifying scholars’ habits and correcting literary style their foremost duties. Those with discernment recognize that unspoiled customs are returning and that this literary tradition is being restored to its ancient standard. Having received our commission, we, his servants, have been apprehensive day and night, fearing only that we might fail to find men worthy of fulfilling His Majesty’s intentions. Thus we have ventured to devote our limited abilities fully to the task. In this examination, we have selected only writing whose reasoning is clear and whose expression conveys its meaning; obscure, recondite, superficial, and florid writing of the sort described above has been excluded. Our purpose is to show candidates the direction they should take, so that they may understand that the practical usefulness of writing lies in this approach, not the other. May this prove beneficial!
We have also heard that the kings of old, in establishing good government, alternated between substance and refinement: when substance predominated, they supplemented it with refinement; when refinement predominated, they corrected it with substance. Literary refinement flourishes in the Southern Metropolitan Region, but I, your servant, fear that its substance has yet to attain the requisite level…

Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination, the twenty-second year of Jiajing (1543).

Proctors

Wu Han, Prefect of Yingtian Prefecture, had the courtesy name Shoufu. Registered with Henan Guard in Henan, he was a native of Wu County in Zhili and a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the xinsi year.

Wang Xueyi, Grand Master for Central Compliance and Vice Prefect of Yingtian Prefecture, had the courtesy name Yuqing. He was a native of Anfu County, Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the jichou year.

Examiners

Hua Cha, Reader-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Ziqian. He was a native of Wuxi County in Zhili and a metropolitan graduate of the bingxu year.

Min Rulin, Right Mentor of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Compiler in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Shiwang. He was a native of Wucheng County, Zhejiang, and a metropolitan graduate of the renchen year.

Associate Examiners

Wang Cong, Instructor in the Confucian School of Li Subprefecture, Yuezhou Prefecture, Huguang, had the courtesy name Tingqi. He was a native of Changle County, Fujian, and a tribute scholar (gongshi) of the jiawu year.

Zhou Tingcong, Instructor in the Confucian School of Fu Subprefecture, Chongqing Prefecture, Sichuan, had the courtesy name Guoyong. He was a native of Chen Subprefecture, Huguang, and a tribute scholar of the gengzi year.

Liang Yanjin, Instructor in the Confucian School of Shanghang County, Tingzhou Prefecture, Fujian, had the courtesy name Jiongfu. He was a native of Dongguan County, Guangdong, and a tribute scholar of the yiyou year.

Cai Mi, Instructor in the Confucian School of Wengyuan County, Shaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong, had the courtesy name Kongzhang. He was a native of Jinxian County, Jiangxi, and a tribute scholar of the dingyou year.

Chen Jiying, Instructor in the Confucian School of Chongyi County, Nan'an Prefecture, Jiangxi, had the courtesy name Yongming. He was a native of Haiyang County, Guangdong, and a tribute scholar of the jiawu year.

Chen Yue, Instructor in the Confucian School of Linxiang County, Yuezhou Prefecture, Huguang, had the courtesy name Qishi. He was a native of Chaoyang County, Guangdong, and a tribute scholar of the jiawu year.

Wang Zhongyu, Instructor in the Confucian School of Cao County, Cao Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, had the courtesy name Gancheng. He was a native of Anfu County, Jiangxi, and a tribute scholar of the dingyou year.

Liu Wei, Instructor in the Confucian School of Xin'an County, Henan Prefecture, Henan, had the courtesy name Yiqing. He was a native of Dai Subprefecture, Shanxi, and a tribute scholar of the dingyou year.

Examination Monitoring Officials

Zhang Cuncheng, Gentleman of the Forest of Literature and Investigating Censor of the Shandong Circuit at Nanjing, had the courtesy name Tishi. He was a native of Raoping County, Guangdong, and a tribute scholar of the renwu year.

第壹場

四書

仁者先難而後獲，可謂仁矣。

今夫天，斯昭昭之多；及其無窮也，日月星辰繫焉，萬物覆焉。今夫地，一撮土之多；及其廣厚，載華嶽而不重，振河海而不洩，萬物載焉。

武王不泄邇，不忘遠。

易

乾始能以美利利天下，不言所利，大矣哉！

大哉乾乎！剛健中正，純粹精也。

王假有廟，利見大人，亨，利貞。用大牲吉，利有攸往。

備物致用，立成器以爲天下利，莫大乎聖人。

二與四同功而異位，其善不同。二多譽，四多懼，近也。柔之爲道，不利遠者；其要无咎，其用柔中也。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“The benevolent person puts difficult tasks first and their rewards afterward. Such a person may be called benevolent.”

“Now Heaven is, in one respect, merely this expanse of brightness; yet in its boundlessness, the sun, moon, and stars are suspended within it, and all things are covered by it. Now Earth is, in one respect, merely a handful of soil; yet in its breadth and thickness, it bears Mount Hua without feeling its weight, holds the rivers and seas without letting them leak away, and supports all things.”

“King Wu did not slight those near him, nor forget those far away.”

Book of Changes (Yi)

“Qian, the Creative, originates things and can benefit all under Heaven with its excellent bounty, without declaring what it benefits. Great indeed is it!”

“Great indeed is Qian! Firm and vigorous, central and correct, pure and unalloyed: it is the quintessence.”

“The king approaches his ancestral temple. It is favorable to see the great man. Success; it is favorable to remain steadfast and correct. Using a large sacrificial animal brings good fortune. It is favorable to have somewhere to go.”

“In preparing things for use and creating finished implements for the benefit of all under Heaven, none surpasses the sage.”

“The second and fourth lines have the same function but occupy different positions, and their merits differ. The second receives much praise; the fourth has much to fear because it is near the ruler. The way of the yielding does not favor being far away; yet its essential aim is to remain without blame, and its effective application lies in being yielding and central.”

The people’s future now depends on your reverently following your accomplished deceased father, carrying on the teachings you have heard and clothing yourself in virtue. Spring and Autumn Annals

Men of Zhu and Zheng attacked Song. 〔Fifth year of Duke Yin〕

In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, fortifications were built at Chuqiu. 〔Second year of Duke Xi〕 In summer, in the fourth month, on the jisi day, the Marquis of Jin and the armies of Qi, Song, and Qin fought the men of Chu at Chengpu. In winter, in the eleventh month, the Marquis of Jin sent Xun Geng on a diplomatic visit to our court, and the Marquis of Wei sent Sun Liangfu on a diplomatic visit to our court. On the bingwu day, we made a covenant with Xun Geng; on the dingwei day, we made a covenant with Sun Liangfu. 〔Third year of Duke Cheng〕

The movements of the Five Phases exhaust one another in turn. The Five Phases, the four seasons, and the twelve months serve in rotation as the foundation for one another; the five notes, the six pitch standards, and the twelve pitch pipes serve in rotation as the fundamental gong tone; the five flavors, the six harmonizations, and the twelve foods serve in rotation as the basic substance; the five colors, the six patterns, and the twelve garments serve in rotation as the basic substance. Thus human beings are the heart of Heaven and Earth and the culmination of the Five Phases: they live by consuming flavors, distinguishing sounds, and clothing themselves in colors.
When the ruler acts, the Recorder of the Left records it; when he speaks, the Recorder of the Right records it. The attendant blind musicians scrutinize the high and low tones of his voice.
To govern all under Heaven through bowing and yielding is what is meant by ritual and music.
Therefore, the gentleman does not use his own abilities to fault others, nor does he shame others for what they cannot do.

藏而設史官以任紀載之事事莫有重

punctuated:
皇天上帝冊表，帝鑒居歆，羣臣表賀。皇上聖不自居，乃於郊祀慶成之日，特下勅宣諭羣臣。其微詞奧旨，表裏六經，嗣徽烈祖，敬天法祖，蓋兩盡焉。是二制者，頒自天府，播之臣民，諸士蓋熟誦而精思之矣。能篇舉而繹其義乎？夫所貴乎士者，不徒談經稽古已也。舉一代之典章，以昭我聖明之謨訓，肆對揚之，無讓。

問：古之有國家者，必置祕書以備典籍之藏，而設史官以任紀載之事，事莫有重焉者也。後世有建藏書之策、下求書之詔，又有四庫之目、三館之儲者，其爲史
translation_en:
…a formal memorial to August Heaven, the Supreme Lord. The Supreme Lord graciously regarded and accepted the offering, and the assembled officials submitted memorials of congratulation. His Majesty, declining to claim sageliness for himself, specially issued an edict instructing the assembled officials on the day celebrating the successful completion of the suburban sacrifice. Its subtle wording and profound purport accord with the Six Classics, inwardly and outwardly, and carry forward the illustrious example of his glorious ancestor. Revering Heaven and emulating his ancestor are thus both fully realized. These two imperial pronouncements were issued from the imperial repository and disseminated among officials and people. You scholars have surely recited them thoroughly and pondered them closely. Can you set forth each text and elucidate its meaning? What is valued in a scholar is more than merely discussing the classics and investigating antiquity. Cite the institutions and regulations of our dynasty to illuminate the plans and instructions of our sagacious sovereign. Expound and extol them fully in your responses, without holding back.

Question: In antiquity, rulers of states invariably established repositories for the storage of canonical and other writings, and appointed historiographers to undertake the work of recording events. No undertaking was more important. In later ages, there were proposals to build book collections and edicts seeking books; there were also catalogues of the Four Repositories and holdings of the Three Institutes. As for their compilation of history…

有起居注有時政記有日曆者此其法
果皆盡善歟我
太祖高皇帝立國之初嘗下令以求遺書及天
下旣定即命官以修日曆
聖謨之弘遠可槩見矣諸生亦能言其大畧否
歟今
國家重熙累洽文治日興顧於是二者乃若
有未暇焉蓋
中祕之圖籍藏之有年或虞其不免於散逸
===
累朝之實錄充棟而議者猶病史文之疎畧
也兹欲悉舉而正之以還
國初之盛若之何而可
聖天子法古右文爲治矧此又關於繼述之大

極言之將以轉

punctuated:
有起居注，有時政記，有日曆者，此其法果皆盡善歟？我太祖高皇帝立國之初，嘗下令以求遺書；及天下旣定，即命官以修日曆。聖謨之弘遠，可槩見矣。諸生亦能言其大畧否歟？今國家重熙累洽，文治日興，顧於是二者，乃若有未暇焉。蓋中祕之圖籍，藏之有年，或虞其不免於散逸；累朝之實錄充棟，而議者猶病史文之疎畧也。兹欲悉舉而正之，以還國初之盛，若之何而可？聖天子法古右文爲治，矧此又關於繼述之大者，而可無以處之歟？諸生苟有所見，願極言之，將以轉聞於上。
問：經傳之微詞奧義，□經大儒而剖析
translation_en:
…there were Diaries of Activity, Records of Current Government, and Daily Calendars. Were all these methods indeed entirely satisfactory? At the founding of the state, our Emperor Taizu Gao once issued an order seeking surviving books; once the realm had been pacified, he appointed officials to compile a Daily Calendar. From this one may discern the breadth and foresight of his sagely plans. Can you candidates also explain their general outlines? Today, as the dynasty enjoys successive eras of prosperity and peace and governance through civil culture flourishes daily, it nevertheless seems that these two matters have not yet received attention. The maps and books in the palace collections have been stored for many years, and there is some fear that they may suffer dispersal and loss. The Veritable Records of successive reigns fill whole buildings, yet critics still deplore the sketchiness of their historical accounts. If we now wish to take up all these matters and rectify them, restoring the flourishing conditions of the dynasty’s beginnings, how might this be accomplished? The sage Son of Heaven governs by following antiquity and honoring literary culture. Since these matters also bear upon the great duty of carrying forward his predecessors’ work, can they be left unattended? If you candidates have insights, please state them fully, so that they may be conveyed to His Majesty.
Question: The subtle expressions and profound meanings of the classics and their commentaries have [an illegible character makes the wording uncertain here: ?] been analyzed by great Confucian scholars…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
明白無餘蘊矣然前乎此者未嘗無近
道之言而後乎此者亦多自得之見是
固學者所當知也試舉數端與諸士揚
確之如表中庸為道統之傳卓識也然
蕭梁之世有述其義者矣指清心為出
治之本至論也然宇文周之時有為此
說者矣敬之一言心法也而魏人已論
於法象之篇權之一字絕學也而唐臣
已辨於易鎮之疏漢詔之敕東平傳相
===
者或謂此等語有所自來晉人之序左
氏春秋者或謂循其言可以入道以至
圖書經緯之言陰陽九六之義五聲六
律十二管還相為宮之說君子皆有取
焉之數人者未嘗聞道於大儒而其言
之相契如此亦有所本歟又如大學格
致之傳補之者當矣而或謂本無所闕
周禮冬官之文不傳久矣而或謂實未
嘗亡論詩者則謂召南之篇有他詩之

punctuated: 明白無餘蘊矣。然前乎此者，未嘗無近道之言；而後乎此者，亦多自得之見。是固學者所當知也。試舉數端，與諸士揚確之。如表《中庸》為道統之傳，卓識也，然蕭梁之世有述其義者矣；指清心為出治之本，至論也，然宇文周之時有為此說者矣。敬之一言，心法也，而魏人已論於《法象》之篇；權之一字，絕學也，而唐臣已辨於易鎮之疏。漢詔之敕東平傳相者，或謂此等語有所自來；晉人之序《左氏春秋》者，或謂循其言可以入道。以至圖書經緯之言，陰陽九六之義，五聲六律十二管還相為宮之說，君子皆有取焉。之數人者，未嘗聞道於大儒，而其言之相契如此，亦有所本歟？又如《大學》格致之傳，補之者當矣，而或謂本無所闕；《周禮》冬官之文，不傳久矣，而或謂實未嘗亡。論《詩》者則謂《召南》之篇有他詩之
translation_en:
…clearly, leaving no hidden meaning unexplained. Yet those who came before this were not without sayings that approached the Way, while those who came afterward also had many insights attained through their own understanding. These are certainly things that scholars ought to know. Let us raise several points and examine them together with you gentlemen.

To single out the Doctrine of the Mean as transmitting the succession of the Way was an outstanding insight; yet already under the Xiao house of Liang there were those who expounded its meaning. To identify purification of the mind as the foundation of governance was a consummate judgment; yet already under the Yuwen house of Zhou there were those who advanced this view. Reverent attentiveness is a method for cultivating the mind, yet a man of Wei had already discussed it in the chapter “Models and Images.” Discretionary judgment is a learning whose transmission had been lost, yet a Tang minister had already distinguished its meaning in a memorial on changing a military command. Concerning the Han edict admonishing the tutor [?] and chancellor of Dongping, some say that expressions of this kind had an antecedent. Concerning a Jin writer’s preface to Zuo’s Spring and Autumn Annals, some say that following its words enables one to enter the Way. Even statements about the interwoven patterns of the River Chart and Luo Writing, the meanings of yin and yang and of nine and six, and the explanation of how the five notes, six pitch standards, and twelve pitch pipes take turns serving as the gong, or fundamental note—all offer something that the cultivated gentleman can adopt. These several men had never learned the Way from the great Confucian masters, yet their words accorded with theirs to such a degree. Did they too have some foundation for their views?

Again, it was fitting to supply the commentary on investigating things and extending knowledge in the Great Learning, yet some maintain that there was originally no omission. The text concerning the Winter Offices in the Rites of Zhou has long ceased to be transmitted, yet some maintain that it was never actually lost. Those who discuss the Book of Odes maintain that the “Airs of Shaonan” contain material from other poems…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
錯簡言易者則云諸卦文言多散逸而
僅存著日抄者有擬於先天之圖作通
考者有取於小序之說若
本朝諸名卿之著述亦有曰私抄曰意見曰
詩考是果有所見而言之歟今程朱之
學天下宗焉而彼諸儒之說則往往置
之不省或譁而攻之蓋雷同相從隨聲
是非乃眾庶之所為耳非所望於豪傑
之士也請悉言之以觀所蘊
===
問有一代之興必有一代之史詳則文繁
畧則事遺作史之難尚矣姑以唐宋論
之唐有天下歷年不及三百而宋僅過
焉其間所可紀者宜與漢不甚相遠也
何唐書既倍於漢而宋史復倍於唐夫
豈時之使然耶抑亦作者不得其法也
唐書成於石晉而重脩於宋遂有新舊
之分不知新書之作果勝於舊否乎當
時表奏之語謂事增於前文省於舊作

本朝諸名卿之著述亦有曰私抄曰意見曰

punctuated:
錯簡。言易者則云諸卦文言多散逸而僅存。著日抄者有擬於先天之圖，作通考者有取於小序之說。若本朝諸名卿之著述，亦有曰私抄，曰意見，曰詩考，是果有所見而言之歟？今程朱之學，天下宗焉，而彼諸儒之說，則往往置之不省，或譁而攻之。蓋雷同相從，隨聲是非，乃眾庶之所為耳，非所望於豪傑之士也。請悉言之，以觀所蘊。

問：有一代之興，必有一代之史。詳則文繁，畧則事遺，作史之難尚矣。姑以唐宋論之，唐有天下，歷年不及三百，而宋僅過焉。其間所可紀者，宜與漢不甚相遠也。何唐書既倍於漢，而宋史復倍於唐？夫豈時之使然耶？抑亦作者不得其法也？唐書成於石晉，而重脩於宋，遂有新舊之分。不知新書之作，果勝於舊否乎？當時表奏之語，謂事增於前，文省於舊。作
translation_en:
…misplaced slips from other poems. Those who discuss the Changes say that much of the Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan) for the various hexagrams has been lost, with only a little surviving. The author of Daily Notes (Richao) offered something modeled on the Diagram of the Prior Heaven; the author of Comprehensive Examination (Tongkao) adopted some explanations from the Minor Prefaces. Among the writings of eminent ministers of our own dynasty are also works called Private Notes (Sichao), Opinions (Yijian), and Examination of the Odes (Shikao). Were these indeed written on the basis of genuine insights? Today, all under Heaven revere the learning of Cheng and Zhu, yet the explanations of those other scholars are often set aside without examination, or assailed with a clamor of criticism. Merely echoing others and following their lead, approving or condemning according to what others say, is only the conduct of ordinary people; it is not what we expect of outstanding scholars. Please discuss these matters fully, so that we may see the learning you possess.

Question: Whenever a dynasty arises, it must have a history. If detailed, the writing becomes voluminous; if concise, events are omitted. The difficulty of writing history has long been recognized. Let us take the Tang and Song as examples. The Tang ruled all under Heaven for fewer than three hundred years, and the Song only slightly exceeded that span. The events worth recording during those periods ought not to differ greatly in number from those of the Han. Why, then, is the History of the Tang already twice the length of the History of the Han, and the History of the Song twice that of the Tang? Was this brought about by the times themselves? Or did the compilers fail to find the proper method? The History of the Tang was completed under the Shi family's Jin dynasty and revised under the Song, giving rise to the distinction between the New and Old histories. Was the New History in fact superior to the Old? The memorial submitted at the time stated that the events recorded had increased over the earlier work, while the text had been reduced from the old version. As for writing…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
史之法果若是乎其所增所省亦可指
而言歟或取乎舊或病乎新又何所見
歟宋史成於胡元泛濫猥俗視舊唐書
尤甚矣然則刋正之舉豈容已哉邇歲
皇上有詔欲刪繁舉要以成新史不知刪繁舉
要與所謂事增文省者同乎異乎何者
為繁何者為要繁何以刪要何以舉豈
無其說乎幸詳陳之以為載筆者之一
助
===
問今百姓乂安海內無事治之極也而北
虜擾我邊鄙則不能免焉此不可不豫
為之備者然其道莫要於足兵足食二
者而已矣往歲俺荅入寇流毒三晉邊
臣輒諉於兵食之不足不其然乎夫沿
邊諸鎮伍籍有定數餽饟有常額
國初之制可謂極善矣乃今兵之所以弱食
之所以匱豈無其故耶夫食以養兵量
兵而後制食也若食不足則兵必多矣

爲繁何者爲要繁何以删要何以舉豈

虜擾我邊鄙則不能免焉此不可不豫

邊諸鎮伍籍有定數餽饟有常額
國初之制可謂極善矣乃今兵之所以弱食
之所以匱豈無其故耶夫食以養兵量
兵而後制食也若食不足則兵必多矣
punctuated:
史之法果若是乎？其所增所省，亦可指而言歟？或取乎舊，或病乎新，又何所見歟？宋史成於胡元，泛濫猥俗，視舊唐書尤甚矣。然則刋正之舉，豈容已哉？邇歲皇上有詔，欲刪繁舉要以成新史。不知刪繁舉要，與所謂事增文省者同乎異乎？何者為繁？何者為要？繁何以刪？要何以舉？豈無其說乎？幸詳陳之，以為載筆者之一助。

問：今百姓乂安，海內無事，治之極也。而北虜擾我邊鄙，則不能免焉。此不可不豫為之備者，然其道莫要於足兵足食二者而已矣。往歲俺荅入寇，流毒三晉，邊臣輒諉於兵食之不足，不其然乎？夫沿邊諸鎮，伍籍有定數，餽饟有常額，國初之制，可謂極善矣。乃今兵之所以弱，食之所以匱，豈無其故耶？夫食以養兵，量兵而後制食也。若食不足，則兵必多矣。
translation_en:
…Is this indeed the proper method of writing history? Can the additions and omissions be specifically identified and discussed? Some favor the old history, while others find fault with the new: what grounds do they have for these judgments? The History of the Song was compiled under the barbarian Yuan dynasty; in its prolixity and vulgarity, it is even worse than the Old History of the Tang. How, then, could the work of revision and correction be abandoned? In recent years, His Majesty has issued an edict calling for the removal of superfluous material and the presentation of essentials to produce a new history. Is this removal of superfluities and presentation of essentials the same as, or different from, what was called “increasing the matters recorded while reducing the wording”? What counts as superfluous, and what as essential? How should superfluities be removed, and how should essentials be presented? Surely there are principles to explain this? Please set them out in detail, to provide some assistance to those who wield the historian’s brush.

Question: Today the common people are orderly and at peace, and all within the seas is free from disturbance: this is the highest achievement of government. Yet we still cannot prevent the northern barbarians from harassing our borderlands. We must prepare for this in advance, and nothing is more important to such preparation than these two things: sufficient troops and sufficient provisions. In past years, Anda invaded and spread devastation through the Three Jin regions of Shanxi. The officials on the frontier invariably blamed insufficient troops and provisions. Was this not so? The garrisons along the frontier have fixed numbers on their military rolls and regular quotas of provisions. The arrangements established at the founding of the dynasty may be called exceedingly good. Surely there are reasons why the troops are now weak and provisions depleted? Provisions sustain the troops; their allocation is determined after the number of troops has been assessed. If provisions are insufficient, then there must be too many troops.…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
兵不足則食必有餘矣二者竝耗其故
又何歟
皇上軫念邊防嘗調客兵以援之發
內帑以濟之邇者又
命廷臣集議以圖惟後備誠慮之周而備之
豫矣不知客兵之調
內帑之發可以爲常否乎建議者無慮數十
其大端則曰招募曰團結曰鹽法曰屯
田是四者果皆得其要否歟古之人有
===
行之者其利害成敗可舉而言歟即行
是四者而兵食可遂足歟抑別有其道
歟諸士咸有先憂之志者也言及之而
不言可乎

punctuated: 兵不足，則食必有餘矣。二者竝耗，其故又何歟？皇上軫念邊防，嘗調客兵以援之，發內帑以濟之。邇者又命廷臣集議，以圖惟後備，誠慮之周而備之豫矣。不知客兵之調、內帑之發，可以爲常否乎？建議者無慮數十，其大端則曰招募，曰團結，曰鹽法，曰屯田。是四者果皆得其要否歟？古之人有行之者，其利害成敗，可舉而言歟？即行是四者，而兵食可遂足歟？抑別有其道歟？諸士咸有先憂之志者也，言及之而不言，可乎？
translation_en:
…If troops are insufficient, provisions must surely be in surplus. Yet both are depleted: what explains this?

His Majesty, deeply concerned about frontier defense, has dispatched troops from elsewhere as reinforcements and disbursed funds from the Privy Treasury to provide relief. Recently he again ordered the court officials to deliberate jointly on preparations for the future. His concern is indeed comprehensive, and his preparations made well in advance. Yet can the dispatch of outside troops and the disbursement of funds from the Privy Treasury be maintained as regular measures?

Those offering proposals number several dozen. Their principal recommendations are recruiting troops, organizing local defense units, reforming the salt administration, and establishing military agricultural colonies. Do all four truly address the essentials? People in antiquity put these measures into practice: can you enumerate and discuss their benefits and drawbacks, successes and failures? If these four measures were implemented, would troops and provisions then become sufficient? Or is there another way?

You candidates all aspire to take thought for public troubles before others do. When this subject has been raised, can you remain silent?

聖人即仁者之心以言仁欲賢者之知所求也

聖人即仁者之心以言仁，欲賢者之知所求也。蓋先難後獲，仁者之心也。外是心以求仁，夫豈知仁者哉？昔夫子因樊遲問仁而告之，若曰：「仁體萬事而統於一心，求仁者亦惟因其事而察其心耳。是故天下之事，凡職分之所當為者，豈無所難乎？仁者則以事之不可已也而先焉，果確之志克勵於向往之初。人之於事，凡躬行之所已及者，寧無所得乎？仁者則以效之不可必
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“The benevolent person puts difficulties first and gains afterward: such a person may be called benevolent.”
Chen Shi

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: Most writers in this examination have explained putting difficulties first and gains afterward in terms of how to practice benevolence, which quite misses the passage’s original purport. This essay alone develops its explanation in terms of responding to affairs and has grasped the meaning. It is therefore recorded as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liang, Instructor: It succeeds in bringing out the heart of the benevolent person.

Comment by Examiner Min, Right Companion of the Heir Apparent: Its wording and meaning are precise: this is the meaning of the Analects.

Comment by Examiner Hua, Reader-in-Waiting: Here is someone with whom one may discuss benevolence.

The sage spoke of benevolence through the heart of the benevolent person, wishing worthy people to know what they should seek. For putting difficulties first and gains afterward is the heart of the benevolent person. If one seeks benevolence apart from this heart, how could one understand the benevolent person?

Once, when Fan Chi asked about benevolence, the Master instructed him, as if to say: “Benevolence gives substance to the myriad affairs and unites them in a single heart. Those who seek benevolence need only examine that heart through those affairs. Thus, among the affairs of the world, can those that fall within one’s proper duties be without difficulties? Yet the benevolent person gives them precedence because they cannot be left undone; a firm and resolute purpose is vigorously cultivated from the very outset of aspiration. In people’s dealings with affairs, can what they have already accomplished through personal practice yield no gains? Yet the benevolent person, because results cannot be assured …

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也而後焉歆羨之情不萌於率履之際道之所
在有人所不能爲者而爲之自强不息未嘗或
急於近利也責之所在有人所不敢爲者而爲
之獨立不懼未嘗豫計其成功也夫曰先難則
易不足言矣曰後獲則失亦勿恤矣仁者之心
如此而何以謂之仁乎蓋仁與不仁之分公私
理欲之間而已苟未事而先畏其難方事而遽
期其效則立心之始已涉於私而充類之盡必
縱夫欲去仁也遠矣今惟先其所難而後其所
===
獲則道心爲主私不得以滅公德性用事欲不
至於間理廓然大公全體於是乎呈露矣物來
順應大用於是乎顯行矣謂之曰仁不亦可乎
須也有志於仁亦求之吾心而已矣大抵學莫
先於義利之辨二者間不容髮而王伯之途君
子小人之類所由以判其幾甚微而其究甚大
故夫子他日於樊遲崇德之問復致意焉蓋雖
因病藥之而聖門之教端不外是後世學術旣
湮而董子正誼明道之說庶幾近之論者謂三

punctuated: 也而後焉，歆羨之情不萌於率履之際。道之所在，有人所不能爲者而爲之，自强不息，未嘗或急於近利也；責之所在，有人所不敢爲者而爲之，獨立不懼，未嘗豫計其成功也。夫曰先難，則易不足言矣；曰後獲，則失亦勿恤矣。仁者之心如此，而何以謂之仁乎？蓋仁與不仁之分，公私理欲之間而已。苟未事而先畏其難，方事而遽期其效，則立心之始已涉於私，而充類之盡必縱夫欲，去仁也遠矣。今惟先其所難，而後其所獲，則道心爲主，私不得以滅公；德性用事，欲不至於間理。廓然大公，全體於是乎呈露矣；物來順應，大用於是乎顯行矣。謂之曰仁，不亦可乎？須也有志於仁，亦求之吾心而已矣。大抵學莫先於義利之辨，二者間不容髮，而王伯之途、君子小人之類所由以判，其幾甚微，而其究甚大。故夫子他日於樊遲崇德之問，復致意焉。蓋雖因病藥之，而聖門之教端不外是。後世學術旣湮，而董子正誼明道之說庶幾近之。論者謂三
translation_en:
…and so he puts the gains afterward; no longing for them arises as he carries out his duties. Where the Way lies, he does what others cannot do, strengthening himself without cease and never hastening after immediate profit. Where responsibility lies, he does what others dare not do, standing alone without fear and never calculating his success in advance. To speak of putting difficulty first leaves what is easy scarcely worth mentioning; to speak of putting gains afterward means that even losses need cause no concern. Such is the mind of the benevolent person, but why may this be called benevolence? The distinction between benevolence and its absence lies simply between public-mindedness and selfishness, between principle and desire. If, before undertaking a task, one already fears its difficulty, and, just as one begins it, one hastily expects results, then the mind’s initial intention is already tainted with selfishness. Carried through to its fullest extent, this must lead to indulging desire: how far removed from benevolence! Only by putting the difficulties first and the gains afterward does the mind of the Way govern, so that selfishness cannot extinguish public-mindedness. The moral nature directs action, so that desire cannot interfere with principle. Expansive and wholly impartial, benevolence thus reveals its entire substance; responding fittingly as things arise, it thus manifests its great functioning. Is it not fitting to call this benevolence? You, Xu, aspire to benevolence; you need only seek it within your own mind.

In learning, nothing takes precedence over distinguishing righteousness from profit. The two are separated by a gap that will not admit a hair, yet this is what divides the paths of the true king and the hegemon, and distinguishes the gentleman from the petty person. The incipient difference is exceedingly subtle, but its ultimate consequences are exceedingly great. Thus, on another occasion, when Fan Chi asked about exalting virtue, the Master again emphasized this point. Although he prescribed a remedy suited to the particular ailment, the teaching of the sage’s school indeed goes no further than this. In later ages, when the tradition of learning had become obscured, Master Dong’s teaching of rectifying righteousness and illuminating the Way came close to it. 中庸極言天地生物之功，一誠之所為也。夫天位乎上，地位乎下，其生物可謂盛矣。然非誠，何以能之哉？中庸二十六章發明天道，至此謂夫天地聖人，一而已矣。欲知至誠無息之功用，盍觀天地之生物乎？今夫天，確然而在上也，自其一處觀之，斯昭昭之多耳。昭昭之多，固莫非天
translation_en:
…after the Three Dynasties, Zhongshu alone was a thoroughly orthodox Confucian of the Han. Is this not indeed true?

“Now Heaven is merely this expanse of brightness; yet in its infinity, the sun, moon, and stars are suspended in it, and all things are covered by it. Now Earth is merely a handful of soil; yet in its breadth and depth, it bears Mount Hua without feeling its weight, contains the rivers and seas without letting them leak away, and supports all things.”

Zhu Dashao

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: “The topic is long. The difficulty lies not in elaborating it, but in drawing it together. This composition is economical in words yet complete in meaning. Accept it.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: “Neither vague nor verbose: this is a fine exposition of the Way of Heaven and Earth.”

Comment by Examiner Min, Right Mentor: “Classical and elegant.”

Comment by Examiner Hua, Reader-in-Waiting: “Precise and apt.”

The Doctrine of the Mean fully expounds Heaven and Earth’s work of bringing forth living things: it is accomplished by sincerity alone. Heaven occupies its place above, and Earth its place below; their generation of living things may indeed be called abundant. Yet without sincerity, how could they accomplish it? Chapter twenty-six of the Doctrine of the Mean elucidates the Way of Heaven, reaching here the point that Heaven, Earth, and the sage are one. If we wish to understand the efficacy of utmost sincerity operating without cessation, why not observe Heaven and Earth bringing forth living things? Now Heaven stands firmly above us. Viewed from any one spot, it is merely this expanse of brightness. This expanse of brightness is assuredly all Heaven…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也而天豈止於是乎由是而及其全體之大穹
窿浩蕩推之莫窮其際也而生物之功顯矣但
見日月之著明也一往一來繫之以乆照焉星
辰之森列也或隱或見繫之以成章焉以至物
類之繁雖以萬計也無不肖形於丕冒之下資
之以始者其資之以覆乎是繫之覆之者天也
而所以繫所以覆天不得而尸之也必有主宰
於其間者矣今夫地隤然而在下也自其一處
觀之一撮土之多耳一撮土之多固莫非地也
===
而地豈止於是乎由是而及其全體之大廣博
深厚探之莫究其垠也而生物之功著矣但見
峙而爲華嶽也載之而不重恢恢乎有餘力焉
流而爲河海也振之而不洩優優乎有餘量焉
以至物類之繁雖有萬殊也無不呈象於大受
之上資之以生者其資之以載乎是載之振之
者地也而所以載所以振地不得而尸之也必
有綱維於其間者矣吁天地以誠而生物如此

translation_en: …yet how could Heaven be limited to this? Proceeding from this to the greatness of its entire extent, we find its vault vast and boundless: however far we trace it, we cannot reach its limits. Thus its work of bringing forth things becomes manifest. We see the brilliant sun and moon, one departing as the other arrives, suspended there to shine enduringly; the densely arrayed stars, now hidden and now visible, suspended there to form celestial patterns. As for the multitude of creatures, though numbered in the tens of thousands, all take shape beneath its vast covering. Does that which provides for their beginning not also provide for their shelter? It is Heaven that suspends and shelters them; yet Heaven itself cannot claim mastery over that by which it suspends and shelters them. There must be something governing within it. Now Earth lies placidly below. Viewed in any one place, it is merely a handful of soil. A handful of soil is certainly part of Earth, yet how could Earth be limited to this? Proceeding from this to the greatness of its entire extent, we find it broad and deep: however far we explore it, we cannot discover its bounds. Thus its work of bringing forth things becomes evident. We see Mount Hua rising aloft: Earth bears it without feeling its weight, ample in its strength, with strength to spare. We see the rivers and seas flowing: Earth holds them without letting them leak away, abundant in its capacity, with capacity to spare. As for the multitude of creatures, though they differ in ten thousand ways, all display their forms upon its all-receiving expanse. Does that which provides for their growth not also provide for their support? It is Earth that bears and holds them; yet Earth itself cannot claim mastery over that by which it bears and holds them. There must be something maintaining order within it. Ah! Such is the way Heaven and Earth bring forth things through sincerity. Can we not see therein the efficacy of utmost sincerity, which never ceases? To consider the matter further, the sage…

translation_en:
…his efficacy indeed stands alongside that of Heaven and Earth. Yet there are things that Heaven and Earth cannot fully accomplish: upon whom could they rely but the sage? Thus, when a sage arises and the Kingly Way prevails, the sun, moon, and stars follow their courses; mountains do not collapse and rivers do not overflow; the common people are transformed, and birds, beasts, fish, and turtles all thrive in due order. In regulating and completing the workings of Heaven and Earth, and assisting their operation, does the sage merely accord with their virtue? Hence it is said: “Heaven and Earth establish their positions; the sage brings their capacities to completion.” Ah! These may indeed be called words that aptly describe the sage.

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
爲然而武王則亦有然者矣彼天下之事有邇
者焉人情藐於不足畏而泄之者多矣武王則
以邇者勢也無邇而不存者道也道之所在其
容以或泄乎故情雖甚親也而臨之以莊地雖
甚密也而居之以愼小物必勤動息其有養也
細行必矜周旋其無虧也蓋其寅恭之誠每嚴
於耳目之所常接而無一毫之敢泄焉是何也
聖人之心入於無内其視邇也猶其視遠也邇
焉不泄出於邇者又可知矣天下之事有遠者

焉人情置於不暇慮而忘之者多矣武王則以
遠者勢也無遠而不存者道也道之所在其容
以或忘乎故幾雖未形也而不見是圖迹雖未
涉也而無疆是恤擴四海之度訏謨以定其命
也建萬世之策先憂以豫其防也蓋其深長之
思恒周於經歷之所不及而無一息之敢忘焉
是何也聖人之心極於無外其視遠也猶其視
邇也遠焉不忘未至於遠者又可知矣夫不泄

translation_en:
…were so; King Wu was also like this. Among the affairs of the world, some are near at hand. Human nature often leads people to belittle these as unworthy of fear and treat them carelessly. King Wu, however, held that nearness was a matter of circumstance, while the Way was present in everything near at hand. Where the Way is present, how could any carelessness be allowed? Thus, even with those to whom he was most closely attached, he conducted himself with dignity; even in the most private places, he comported himself with caution. He attended diligently to small matters, nurturing himself in both activity and repose; he watched over the smallest details of conduct, allowing no lapse in any of his dealings. His sincere reverence was always exacting toward whatever his eyes and ears regularly encountered, and he dared not permit the slightest carelessness. Why was this? The sage’s mind penetrates inward until nothing remains beyond its inward reach: he regards what is near just as he regards what is distant. Since he was not careless toward what was near, his treatment of what lay beyond the near can readily be inferred.

Among the affairs of the world, some are distant. Human nature often leads people to set these aside as things they have no leisure to consider, and so forget them. King Wu, however, held that distance was a matter of circumstance, while the Way was present in everything distant. Where the Way is present, how could anything be forgotten? Thus, even before the first stirrings of events had taken shape, he planned for what was unseen; even where his footsteps had not reached, his concern knew no bounds. He enlarged his vision to encompass all within the Four Seas, making far-reaching plans to secure his mandate; he established policies for ten thousand generations, anticipating troubles so as to prepare safeguards in advance. His profound and enduring thought always encompassed what lay beyond his own experience, and he dared not forget it for a single moment. Why was this? The sage’s mind reaches outward until nothing lies beyond it: he regards what is distant just as he regards what is near. Since he did not forget what was distant, his treatment of what was less distant can readily be inferred. To avoid carelessness may be possible; to avoid carelessness toward what is near is beyond ordinary ability. To avoid forgetting may be possible; to avoid forgetting…

translation_en:
…but not forgetting those far away is beyond ordinary capacity. Is this not why King Wu possessed flourishing virtue and consummate benevolence, and carried forward the succession of the sages before him? Yet he had received instruction. The admonitions of the Cinnabar Writing and the exposition of the Great Plan show how thoroughly King Wu devoted himself to learning. Thus, when addressing his assembled followers, he warned against favoritism, excessive intimacy, licentiousness, and drunkenness, and remained ever watchful over his bearing, speech, sight, and hearing. In administering government, he made recruiting overlooked worthies and restoring neglected offices urgent priorities, and ensured that routes of communication reached the Nine Yi and Eight Man peoples. In essence, all this arose from his capacity for reverence [?]. Thus it is said: “Reverence is the essential principle of sagely learning from beginning to end.” May those who bear responsibility for all under Heaven understand this!

Book of Changes

text:

以示占其有取於萃之時乎且萃之爲卦以萃
聚爲義時至於萃無所不聚矣占者値此當何
如哉亦曰君臣各盡其道耳是故宗廟者祖考
所依也王者求聚於渙而況處萃乎于以假之
感通妙於幽明之際孝孰大焉是蓋聚其精神
而非漫焉以從事如在之誠斯庶幾耳否則匕
鬯之重誰其主之大人者民物所歸也君子求

translation_en: For the ruler’s service to the spirits and the minister’s service to the ruler each have their proper way. The sage enumerated these to instruct those consulting the oracle: was this not because they accord with the circumstances of Gathering (Cui)? The meaning of the hexagram Gathering is assembling together. When the time of Gathering arrives, there is nothing that does not gather. What should one who encounters this hexagram in divination do? Simply this: ruler and minister must each fully discharge their proper duties. Thus, the ancestral temple is where forefathers find their resting place. A king seeks to gather them even in Dispersion (Huan); how much more so when situated in Gathering! By approaching the temple, he achieves wondrous communion across the boundary between the unseen and visible worlds. What filial piety could be greater? This surely requires concentrating his vital spirit, rather than conducting the service carelessly; only with the sincerity of serving the ancestors as though they were present can he come close to this. Otherwise, who could preside over the weighty responsibilities symbolized by the sacrificial ladle and fragrant wine? The great man is one to whom the people and all things turn. The gentleman seeks deliverance even in Obstruction (Jian); how much more so when situated in Gathering! By going to see the great man, he brings virtue and achievement to fruition through intercourse between those above and those below. What success could surpass this? Yet he must hold to his upright way and must not seek agreement at any cost. Only integrity firm as a rock deserves esteem. Otherwise, who would associate with a faction of partisan accomplices? Approaching the temple is indeed how one presents one’s offerings; but if the rites are incomplete, will the spirits come to partake of them? Thus, the use of two offering vessels is permissible in Decrease (Sun), but not in Gathering. The sacrificial animals must be whole and plump, displaying the abundant resources of the people’s labor. Then one sacrifices and receives blessings: great indeed is the auspiciousness. Otherwise, would this not verge on possessing all under Heaven yet being parsimonious toward one’s parents? Seeing the great man is indeed how one puts one’s righteousness into practice; but if the Way is not realized, does one not enter public service in vain? Thus, withdrawing and keeping one’s virtue concealed is permissible in Stagnation (Pi), but not in Gathering. One must promote the Way and bring about good government, fulfilling the people’s longstanding hopes for their livelihood. translation_en:
…come close to hoarding one's treasure and letting one's state go astray? Why is this? In the ruler's way, nothing is greater than serving the spirits. To provide abundantly when the time permits abundance is not extravagance. In the minister's way, nothing is greater than serving the ruler. To enter service when the time permits action is not wickedness. Such are the words King Wen appended to the hexagram Cui (Gathering Together); his intention to admonish those consulting the oracle is evident. Yet these matters also have a foundation. The people are the mainstay of the spirits. The sage king first brings his people to fulfillment and only afterward devotes his efforts to the spirits. Thus, in gathering people through wealth, does he not embody the way of Cui in his dealings with the people? The person is the conduit of the Way. The gentleman first makes preparations within himself and only afterward puts his capacities to use in the world. Thus, in amply storing up virtue, does he not embody the way of Cui in his own person? Ah! This is the foundation of serving the spirits and serving the ruler, and also the intent of the sage in appending these words.

“Providing things and bringing them into use, establishing finished implements to benefit all under Heaven: in these, none is greater than the sage.”
Cai Huan

此哉大傳贊蓍龜之功用而此以聖人言之謂

用不致不能無棄物矣於是隨其材質之宜而
百物為之備精粗美惡雖其情之不齊而法制
品節使其用之各適焉朝信道而工信度有器

translation_en:
…such undertakings are not easily accomplished. Who, then, other than a sage could take part in providing things and fashioning implements? The Great Commentary praises the efficacy and uses of milfoil stalks and tortoise shells, yet here it speaks of the sage. This means that Heaven and Earth establish their positions, and the sage brings their capacities to fulfillment. By observing the greatness of his creations and institutions, one can understand their efficacy and uses.

Thus Heaven produces the seasons and Earth produces resources: wherever there are things, they necessarily have uses. If their uses are not fully realized, some things will inevitably be wasted. Accordingly, the sage provides the full range of things in accordance with the suitability of their material qualities. Though their inherent qualities differ—fine or coarse, beautiful or ugly—he regulates and orders them through standards and institutions, ensuring that each is put to an appropriate use. The court holds faithfully to the Way, and artisans hold faithfully to measurements: where there are implements, there are benefits. If implements are not established, some benefits will inevitably remain unrealized. Accordingly, after taking the images as his guide, he brings implements to completion and thereby encourages the hundred crafts. Strange skills and excessive ingenuity are not allowed to disrupt his government, while all that pertains to the people's livelihood and daily needs can share in his accomplishments. Who could accomplish such things?

When the intelligent initiate an undertaking, their work may indeed be refined, yet making it capable of continuation is difficult. When the skillful carry it forward, their methods may indeed merit attention, yet they become obstructed when seeking to extend them far. Only the sage possesses acuity and sagely understanding bestowed abundantly by Heaven, and follows these with the exertions of his ears, eyes, mind, and thought in government. He practices the Way of the three weighty responsibilities, adapting to change for the people's benefit; he gathers all around the supreme standard and brings them back to it, so that all within the Four Seas take it as their rule. He magnifies the governance of a king and cultivates the Way to establish instruction; with statutes and standards in place, the myriad generations depend upon them forever. Thus it is said, “None is greater than the sage.” Truly, the sage's creations and institutions lie beyond the reach of mere intelligence and skill. Does this not also reveal the great efficacy and uses of milfoil stalks and tortoise shells?

Nevertheless, milfoil stalks and tortoise shells are things, and divination by shells and stalks is an instrument. The sage illuminates…

…the Way of Heaven and examines the circumstances of the people; when numinous objects appear, he leads the people in their use [?]. This is entirely the sage’s accomplishment. Had methods governing their use not been established, one would likewise have been confined by objects and restricted by implements. punctuated: 適然者謂之時。人君求盡憲天之道，而可不知所從耶？是故吉凶悔吝生乎動，而公私義利起於思。使動不慮善，其動也妄矣。王其獨觀萬化，而研夫可否之幾；精察一心，而謹於危微之辨。「弗慮胡獲」，匪可以成心與也，則方物出謀，而道必稽於無弊；「屢省乃成」，匪可以疑謀叅也，則視履考祥，而政必期於有恒。事有兩端，而惟執其中；善無常主，而求協於一，非慮善以動乎？然不可易者理也，而不可齊者時也。使動不以時，其動也滯矣。又必觀天下之變，而會通以酌其宜；達天下之權，而推移以濟其用。治以道舉，而道有升降，則隨時以為汙隆；政由俗革，而俗有從違，則因時以為損益。時未至也，不先天以開人；時旣至也，不後期而失事，非動惟厥時乎？吁！方動而慮乎善，則心與天一矣；已動而合乎時，則行與天一矣。人君能盡憲天之道如此，而臣民有不欽從者哉？大抵天不能外理，而理不能違時。人君奉若天道，不過順之而已。傳說之告高
translation_en:
…what is fitting to particular circumstances is called timeliness. If a ruler seeks to fulfill the way of taking Heaven as his model, can he fail to know what to follow? Thus good fortune, misfortune, regret, and humiliation arise from action, while public and private interests, righteousness and profit, originate in thought. If one acts without considering what is good, one’s actions will be reckless. Let the king contemplate for himself the myriad transformations and investigate the subtle beginnings that determine what is acceptable and what is not; let him scrutinize his own mind closely and carefully distinguish the precarious human mind from the subtle moral mind. “Without deliberation, what can be gained?” One must not approach this with a preconceived mind. Thus, in assessing things and devising plans, one must examine whether one’s course is free from defects. “Repeated examination brings accomplishment.” One must not introduce doubtful plans into one’s deliberations. Thus, in inspecting one’s conduct and examining its auspicious indications, one must ensure constancy in government. Affairs have two extremes, but one holds fast to the mean between them; goodness has no fixed embodiment, but one seeks accord with the single principle. Is this not to consider what is good before acting?

Yet principle cannot be changed, while circumstances cannot be made uniform. If one acts without regard to the time, one’s actions will be inflexible. One must also observe the changes throughout the world, grasp their connections, and weigh what is appropriate; understand how to weigh expedient courses throughout the world, and adapt so as to make them effective. Order is established through the Way, yet the Way has its rises and declines; accordingly, one adjusts to the times, whether low or flourishing. Government changes in response to customs, yet customs may be compliant or resistant; accordingly, one makes reductions or additions as the times require. When the time has not yet come, one does not anticipate Heaven in initiating human action; when the time has come, one does not miss the appointed moment and let affairs slip. Is this not to act only at the proper time?

Ah! When, on the verge of acting, one considers what is good, one’s mind is at one with Heaven; when one has acted in accord with the time, one’s conduct is at one with Heaven. If a ruler can thus fulfill the way of taking Heaven as his model, could any of his officials or people fail to follow him reverently? In general, Heaven cannot stand outside principle, and principle cannot run counter to the times. For a ruler to honor and follow the Way of Heaven is simply to accord with it. Fu Yue’s [?] admonition to Gao…

translation_en:
…in speaking to Gaozong of goodness and timeliness, [Fu Yue] was surely speaking of accord. Through accord, Heaven and Earth take their proper places and the myriad things flourish; the Way of Heaven then resides in oneself. Yet at Gaozong’s supplementary sacrifice there was still the portent of a crowing pheasant: this was a response to a failure of accord. Alas! Even with Gaozong’s reverent silence and contemplation of the Way, the slightest failure of accord immediately elicited a response. Can a ruler fail to be apprehensive about his actions?

“Bowing with hands joined and knocking their heads to the ground before their sovereign, they said: ‘Set in their places your officers, your governors, and your standards of conduct; herein lies being a sovereign.’”

Jiang Yipeng

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, an Instructor: “The language and spirit are expansive, while the reasoning is subtle and precise. An excellent composition.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, an Instructor: “Reading this, one can vividly perceive the sincerity with which the ministers of Xia addressed their ruler.”

Comment by Examiner Min, Right Companion of the Heir Apparent: “This is someone who speaks well of the ruler’s Way.”

Comment by Examiner Hua, Reader-in-Waiting: “The composition has pivotal connections.”

A great minister recounts how ministers of an earlier age paid reverence to their ruler and thereby urged him to fulfill what makes a ruler. Employing worthy men to achieve good government is the ruler’s Way. Those earlier ministers paid reverence to encourage their ruler: their loyal affection was utmost. It was fitting that the Duke of Zhou should recount this in admonishing King Cheng. It is as though he said: In former times, under Xia, the ruler understood the need for solicitude, and his ministers fully carried out their duty of recommending worthy men. The meaning of their words was that, having already recognized those who practiced the nine virtues, they then came forward to recommend them.

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
先之拜手以致其恭繼之稽首以成其禮非以
導佞也蓋將啓其聽德之聰以致吾忠告之益
耳誠以我后出震繼離巍乎爲上天之子體元
居正赫然爲下民之王可謂尊矣居其位盍思
所以盡其道乎乃復言曰君道以事天爲先而
事天以求賢爲要彼九德之人知而弗用可乎
必宅乃常任使掌事典以經邦國者有其人焉
宅乃牧夫使掌敎典以安邦國者有其人焉宅
乃準人使掌刑典以平邦國者有其人焉量才
===
以授之而詔爵詔祿推誠以任之而弗貳弗疑
夫如此則衆賢盈於朝而下之所圖莫非協恭
之誼官聯會其要而謀之所建一皆熙載之忠
贊襄乎萬幾而天工得其理矣撫綏乎萬邦而
天民得其所矣欽恤乎五刑而天討得其宜矣
爲君之道庶幾克盡而循名責實夫復何忝乎
吁夏臣之告敎其君如此其君之知恤可見矣
吾王可弗念哉抑考臨九五曰知臨大君之宜
吉朱子釋之以爲不自用而任人智之事也夫

吉朱子釋之以爲不自用而任人智之事也夫
punctuated:
先之拜手，以致其恭；繼之稽首，以成其禮。非以導佞也，蓋將啓其聽德之聰，以致吾忠告之益耳。誠以我后出震繼離，巍乎爲上天之子；體元居正，赫然爲下民之王，可謂尊矣。居其位，盍思所以盡其道乎？乃復言曰：「君道以事天爲先，而事天以求賢爲要。彼九德之人，知而弗用，可乎？必宅乃常任，使掌事典以經邦國者有其人焉；宅乃牧夫，使掌敎典以安邦國者有其人焉；宅乃準人，使掌刑典以平邦國者有其人焉。量才以授之，而詔爵詔祿；推誠以任之，而弗貳弗疑。夫如此，則衆賢盈於朝，而下之所圖，莫非協恭之誼；官聯會其要，而謀之所建，一皆熙載之忠。贊襄乎萬幾，而天工得其理矣；撫綏乎萬邦，而天民得其所矣；欽恤乎五刑，而天討得其宜矣。爲君之道，庶幾克盡；而循名責實，夫復何忝乎？」吁！夏臣之告敎其君如此，其君之知恤可見矣。吾王可弗念哉？

抑考《臨》九五曰：「知臨，大君之宜，吉。」朱子釋之，以爲不自用而任人，智之事也。夫
translation_en:
…He first bowed with hands clasped to express his reverence, then bowed his head to the ground to complete the ceremony. This was not to encourage flattery, but to open his ruler’s ears to virtue and make his own loyal counsel beneficial. Indeed, our sovereign comes forth in Zhen and succeeds in Li—the trigrams of thunder and radiance—standing exalted as the son of Heaven above; embodying the primal power and occupying the rightful position, he stands illustrious as king of the people below. His position may truly be called august. Occupying that position, should he not consider how to fulfill its duties? The minister therefore continued: “The ruler’s Way gives precedence to serving Heaven, and the essential means of serving Heaven is to seek worthy men. Can one recognize men possessed of the nine virtues yet fail to employ them? You must place them in your regular offices, so that there are suitable men to administer the statutes governing affairs and thereby order the states; place them as your governors, so that there are suitable men to administer the statutes of instruction and thereby bring peace to the states; and place them as your judicial officials, so that there are suitable men to administer the penal statutes and thereby secure justice in the states. Assess their abilities before assigning them office, and decree their ranks and stipends. Entrust them with responsibilities in complete sincerity, without wavering or suspicion. If you do this, worthy men will fill the court, and everything your subordinates plan will accord with the duty of working together reverently. The offices will coordinate their essential functions, and every proposal they put forward will express loyalty through the successful discharge of their duties. They will assist with the myriad affairs of government, and Heaven’s work will be properly ordered; they will pacify and nurture the myriad states, and Heaven’s people will find their proper places; they will apply the five punishments with reverent care and compassion, and Heaven’s chastisements will be fitting. Thus you may come close to fulfilling the ruler’s Way. When actual performance is measured against the title you bear, what cause for shame will remain?” Ah! Such was the instruction that the minister of Xia gave his ruler; from this we can see that his ruler understood the need for care. Can our king fail to reflect upon it?

text:

人之知識有限而以人之所及濟吾之所不及
則兼聽並觀聰明莫大焉此明四目達四聰舜

以辨賢而用之乎故人君貴豫養聰明之德而
其功則自務學始

translation_en:
…“One truly possessed of clear perception becomes the sovereign”; yet refraining from relying solely upon oneself is considered wisdom. Why is this? One person's knowledge is limited. By drawing upon what others can accomplish to supplement what one cannot, one listens broadly and considers all perspectives: no greater clarity of perception is possible. This is what is meant by “making the four eyes clear and opening the four channels of hearing,” through which Shun achieved good government. Nevertheless, unless a ruler truly possesses clear perception himself, how can he distinguish the worthy and employ them? Thus a ruler must value cultivating this virtue in advance, and the work begins with diligent study.

Book of Odes

“With our pure grain offerings and our sacrificial sheep, we sacrifice to the soil god and the spirits of the four quarters. Our fields have yielded well: this is the farmers' joy. With zithers and the beating of drums, we welcome the Father of Agriculture, praying for sweet rain to aid our millet crops and to nourish our men and women.”

Meng Yuzheng

Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor, comments: “‘To benefit the men and women’ has two meanings: to nourish them and to make them good. Many omit one of these. This composition alone explains them clearly and fully. Moreover, its language throughout is splendid and conforms to classical standards. It is among the finest interpretations of the meaning of the Odes of the Court; I select it for inclusion.”

Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: “The intent of serving the spirits and honoring agriculture in an age of flourishing government overflows beyond the words.”

Examiner Min, Right Mentor, comments: “Ornament and substance alike flourish.”

Examiner Hua, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “It captures the character of gentleness, kindness, sincerity, and generosity.”

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
觀公卿事神之詳而重農之意可見矣夫力田
而獲有年神之賜也報於旣往而祈於將來其
重農之意何如哉此公卿有田禄者力於農事
以奉方社田祖之祭至此若曰有國家者致力
於民所以植厚生之原也致力於神所以爲稔
成之利也我今場功甫畢而報成之典行焉使
物有弗備則不足以達誠欲神之享得乎故潔
齊盛於豆其臭則亶時也登犧羊於俎其色則
從宜也于以祀后土之神而四方之咸徧萬寳
===
告成之秋肅然靈貺之是答矣若此者果何爲
哉誠以田之旣臧也吾固得以享其利矣田之
所以臧也吾不得而與其力焉蓋三時之勞有
以通神明之感而十千之取遂以蒙敷錫之恩
以神之慶及乎農以農之慶及乎我報其可容
已耶歲事方報而祈年之意寓焉使樂有弗盛
則不足以宣和欲神之歆得乎故拊我琴瑟合
之升歌而不亂擊我土鼓比於衆音而克諧于
以迎田祖之神而甘雨之豫祈農祥晨正之日

之升歌而不亂擊我土鼓比於衆音而克諧于
以迎田祖之神而丼雨之豫祈農祥晨正之日
punctuated: 觀公卿事神之詳，而重農之意可見矣。夫力田而獲有年，神之賜也。報於旣往，而祈於將來，其重農之意何如哉！此公卿有田禄者，力於農事，以奉方社田祖之祭，至此若曰：有國家者，致力於民，所以植厚生之原也；致力於神，所以爲稔成之利也。我今場功甫畢，而報成之典行焉。使物有弗備，則不足以達誠，欲神之享得乎？故潔齊盛於豆，其臭則亶時也；登犧羊於俎，其色則從宜也。于以祀后土之神，而四方之咸徧。萬寳告成之秋，肅然靈貺之是答矣。若此者，果何爲哉？誠以田之旣臧也，吾固得以享其利矣；田之所以臧也，吾不得而與其力焉。蓋三時之勞，有以通神明之感，而十千之取，遂以蒙敷錫之恩。以神之慶及乎農，以農之慶及乎我，報其可容已耶？歲事方報，而祈年之意寓焉。使樂有弗盛，則不足以宣和，欲神之歆得乎？故拊我琴瑟，合之升歌而不亂；擊我土鼓，比於衆音而克諧。于以迎田祖之神，而甘雨之豫祈。農祥晨正之日，
translation_en: By observing the meticulous care with which the dukes and ministers serve the spirits, one can see their concern for agriculture. That diligent cultivation yields an abundant year is a gift from the spirits. In offering thanks for what has passed and praying for what is to come, how profound is their concern for agriculture! These dukes and ministers, who receive stipends from landed estates, devote themselves to agricultural affairs in order to perform sacrifices to the spirits of the four directions, the soil, and the Ancestor of Agriculture. At this point, it is as though they were saying: Those who possess states and domains devote their efforts to the people in order to establish the foundation of an ample livelihood; they devote their efforts to the spirits in order to secure the benefits of ripening crops and a completed harvest. Now that our work on the threshing grounds has just concluded, we perform the ceremony of thanksgiving for the harvest. If any offering were lacking, it would be insufficient to convey our sincerity. Could we then expect the spirits to partake? Thus we purify the sacrificial grain in the offering vessels, its fragrance being truly fitting; we place the sacrificial sheep upon the stands, their color conforming to what is appropriate. With these we sacrifice to the spirit of the earth and extend our worship throughout the four directions. In autumn, when all the precious crops have reached maturity, we solemnly repay the blessings of the spirits. What, indeed, is the purpose of all this? It is truly because, once the fields have yielded well, we certainly enjoy their benefits; yet we have contributed no labor to that which made them yield well. The toil of the three farming seasons has moved the spirits to respond, and the yield of ten thousand has thus received the bounty they bestow. Through the spirits’ blessings, benefits reach the farmers; through the farmers’ blessings, benefits reach us. How could we possibly cease offering thanks? Even as we give thanks for the year’s work, the intention to pray for another good harvest is already present. If the music were not magnificent, it would be insufficient to express harmony. Could we then expect the spirits to accept our offerings? Thus we play our qin and se zithers, combining them with the singing in the hall without disorder; we strike our earthen drums, blending them harmoniously with the other sounds. translation_en:
…Heaven’s beneficent rain will descend in abundance. Could such rites possibly be vain? With this rich moisture [?], millet can fully realize its nature; with the abundance yielded by the land, men and women can sustain their lives. Households have stores of grain, and the means of nourishment are thereby complete; people understand ritual and proper conduct, and good customs consequently flourish. The blessings of the spirits reach us, and our blessings reach the farmers: could prayers be delayed even a little? Ah! In giving thanks for this year, they invariably attribute the achievement to the people; in praying for the coming year, they do not reserve the benefits for themselves. How worthy were the dukes and ministers of Zhou! Indeed, Zhou’s concern for agriculture had very ancient origins. It began with Hou Ji, was strengthened under Gong Liu, and was carried forward by Kings Wen and Wu. Never for a single day was it forgotten. This was truly because the state depends upon the people, and the people upon food. Thus the Son of Heaven personally put this into practice above, and all the dukes and ministers were transformed by his example. When the rites of supplication and thanksgiving were performed at their proper times, the people lived in harmony and the spirits sent down blessings. There was good reason for the consummate order throughout the realm! Later generations abandoned their agricultural affairs, and Zhou consequently fell into decline. Alas! The neglect or cultivation of agricultural administration is the turning point between order and disorder. Can one fail to exercise care?

“Brightly illustrious is Zhou; in due order are those who hold office. Shields and dagger-axes are laid away; bows and arrows are put into cases. We seek excellent virtue and spread it throughout this land of Xia. Truly, the king preserves it.”

Shi Zongyi.

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: “The passage explaining ‘preserves it’ is apt and clear. In expressing the meaning of the hymn, nothing surpasses this [?].”

Examiner Min, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent (you zhongyun), comments: Captures the style of the Odes of Praise (Song).

The poet praises the practice of kingly government in a flourishing age, and trusts that it can thereby preserve the Mandate of Heaven. Now, a ruler of men is one who orders all things on behalf of Heaven; if he is able to practice kingly government throughout the realm, then the Mandate of Heaven can be preserved. How fitting it is that the poet recounts and praises this! This is a musical song for royal tours of inspection, court audiences, and sacrificial announcements. It means that the kingly enterprise is not easily accomplished, and that which shows favor to it depends on Heaven; the Mandate of Heaven cannot be taken as constant, and that which preserves it lies in governance. Now our king accords with Heaven to carry out the change of Mandate, and the realm within the seas is clear and bright; he responds to the destined cycle by making timely tours of inspection, and human culture is brilliantly manifest. Illustrious indeed is the House of Zhou—no longer the foulness and turbidity of the final days of Shang! Yet at the beginning of a new era's transformation, at the very moment when men's hearts look on with renewed eyes, what indeed does our king do? Truly, because the myriad states have come to court, the duties of ministers have already been reported. Thereupon he ranks the dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons, distinguishing them so as to wield the authority of awe and blessing. Those who possess virtue and merit, we reward them, and the recompense of adding territories and advancing ranks is carried out; those who are disobedient and irreverent, we reprimand them, and the punishment of reducing territories and stripping titles is enforced. Furthermore, because the four quarters are already pacified, weapons of war need not be used; thereupon he gathers in the shields, spears, bows, and arrows and stores them away, so as to show his intention to give the people rest. title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
倫惇敘於天下也丹書之戒訪於太公而布之
敬義彰著於中國也王政之行如此吾知福善
禍淫天之道也今也賞善而罰惡則欽崇乎天
道者至矣天欲治乎斯世寧不永付吾王以序
位之柄哉好生惡殺天之心也今也偃武而修
文則奉若乎天心者至矣天不遺乎吾人寧不
永托吾王以肆夏之任哉赫赫之命信乎其能
保之而不失也吁詩人以是頌武王亦可謂善
言人君事天之道者矣抑嘗考虞周巡狩之典
===
雖詳畧不同然皆爲民而出非慢遊也故車旗
所至之地人心無弗畏且愛焉畏之而不敢背
愛之而不忍離祈天永命之道在是矣此所以
爲太平有道之盛而周之享國尤過其歷歟後
世若封泰山幸汾陰者縱其侈心以勞民其治
之不古若何怪哉

春秋

translation_en:
…the fundamental human relationships were duly ordered throughout the realm. He consulted Taigong about the admonitions of the Cinnabar Writing and promulgated them, making reverence and righteousness manifest in the Central States. Such was the practice of royal government. I know that blessing the good and bringing calamity upon the wicked is Heaven’s Way. By rewarding goodness and punishing evil, he showed the utmost reverence for Heaven’s Way. Since Heaven desired this world to be well governed, how could it fail to entrust our king forever with the authority to arrange ranks and offices? To cherish life and abhor killing is Heaven’s heart. By laying aside arms and cultivating civil government, he complied fully with Heaven’s heart. Since Heaven does not abandon our people, how could it fail to entrust our king forever with responsibility for extending his rule throughout the Xia lands? He could indeed preserve that illustrious Mandate without losing it. Ah! In praising King Wu in these terms, the poet may truly be said to have expressed well the way in which a ruler serves Heaven.

I have also examined the institutions governing royal inspection tours under Yu and Zhou. Though they differed in elaborateness and simplicity, these journeys were all undertaken for the people, not for idle pleasure. Thus, wherever the royal carriages and banners arrived, the people invariably felt both awe and affection. In awe, they dared not turn against their ruler; in affection, they could not bear to leave him. Herein lay the way to pray to Heaven for an enduring Mandate. Was this not what made theirs a flourishing age of peace and rightful rule, and enabled Zhou in particular to hold the realm beyond its allotted span? As for later rulers who performed the feng sacrifice at Mount Tai or made imperial visits to Fenyin, they indulged their extravagance and exhausted the people. What wonder that their government fell short of antiquity’s?

Spring and Autumn Annals

“In spring, in the first month of the king’s calendar, fortifications were built at Chuqiu.” Second year of Duke Xi.

“In summer, in the fourth month, on the sisi day [?], the Marquis of Jin, the army of Qi, the army of Song, and the army of Qin fought the men of Chu at Chengpu …”

Thus the Classic passes over Duke Huan: it does not list the lords in order, nor does it offer a single favorable phrase to exalt him. It is as though it says: the world may do without the achievement of preserving Wei, but it cannot do without the distinctions of status and duty between ruler and subject.
As for Chu, after Duke Xiang of Song fell, Xiong Yun ran rampant, and the Ji-surnamed states north of the Han River were virtually all extinguished. At that time Duke Wen of Jin presided as hegemon. A true king has armies that proclaim offenses and carry out punitive expeditions; he disdains the deceptive stratagems of the moment. Had Duke Wen, concerned about Chu, dispatched his army according to proper rules, would defeating it not have been good? Instead, he felled trees to make his forces appear more numerous and covered horses with tiger skins. First he detached Chu’s allies and provoked its anger; then he lured its troops into advancing and attacked them when they were off guard. He commanded the troops of the central states yet abandoned the rules of the Minister of War. Judged by the Way and righteousness, his deceit was extreme! Alas! In the campaign of the three mobilizations, they still knew to deal with the enemy sincerely and without haste; yet Duke Wen falls short even by that standard. What can one say of him? Thus, in its entry concerning the Marquis of Jin, the Classic writes “joined battle with,” and likewise offers no favorable phrase to exalt him. It is as though it says: the world may do without the achievement of restraining Chu, but it cannot do without the trustworthiness and righteousness of the central states.

A courtesy visit without a covenant accords with the ritual propriety of the regional lords; arrogating authority and initiating new affairs is no proper conduct for a subject. When the two ministers came to Lu, they should have reflected: “We are indeed observing ritual by making a courtesy visit, not drawing up oaths to conclude a covenant. We need only respectfully present jade and silk and diligently carry out our mission.” Yet scarcely had the gifts in the courtyard been presented when the sacrificial victim and the blood for the oath were hastily set out. They abandoned good faith to impose a binding pledge before the bright spirits, and indulged their desires to violate the statutes of the former kings. What, indeed, were they doing? They knew only that they could exercise discretion beyond their own borders, but did not know that a covenant must be authorized by their ruler. To act without his command is to disregard the ruler. This is called violating righteousness; to violate righteousness is to lack loyalty. Could they escape culpability? Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals does not attach their states’ names to them, thereby condemning their unauthorized action. If this principle prevails, subjects must obey their rulers and sons must obey their fathers, and the proper relations between superiors and inferiors will be set right.

Why say that they set themselves on an equal footing with their superior? Heaven is exalted and earth is lowly: such is the distinction between ruler and subject. To transgress ritual and overstep its bounds is no proper way for one in a subordinate position to behave. When the two ministers wished to conclude a covenant, they should have reflected: “The rulers of all five ranks are rulers, and the subjects distinguished by the three forms of salutation are subjects. We may scrupulously keep to our offices and ranks and bind our peers in alliance.” Yet now they made the ruler of our state stoop to join in this covenant. In the solemn array of ranks, they encroached upon those above them; the graded dignities were perilously undermined from below. Again, what were they doing? This is called violating ritual propriety; to violate ritual propriety is to lack reverence. Could the law pardon them? title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
不得僭天子而上下之禮立矣是則罪其專雖
爲晉衞也所以敎天下爲臣者之忠也罪其抗
雖爲魯也所以敎天下爲臣者之敬也先儒謂
春秋以道名分詎不信夫抑二卿不足責矣魯
秉周禮乃不能陳大義以却之何其弱乎傳稱
二卿將尋盟公疑其位次而臧宣叔爰稽古制
以對其言辨矣而獨於諸侯大夫之不可同盟
卒無一言及之察於節目而昧其大體甚哉其
不知務也嗟乎吾於魯之君臣不能無憾
===

之上下

之意此作盡之

punctuated:
不得僭天子，而上下之禮立矣。是則罪其專，雖爲晉衞也，所以敎天下爲臣者之忠也；罪其抗，雖爲魯也，所以敎天下爲臣者之敬也。先儒謂《春秋》以道名分，詎不信夫？抑二卿不足責矣，魯秉周禮，乃不能陳大義以却之，何其弱乎！傳稱二卿將尋盟，公疑其位次，而臧宣叔爰稽古制以對，其言辨矣，而獨於諸侯大夫之不可同盟，卒無一言及之。察於節目而昧其大體，甚哉其不知務也！嗟乎！吾於魯之君臣不能無憾。

禮記
「動則左史書之，言則右史書之，御瞽幾聲之上下。」
曹三暘
同考試官學正周批：「王者檢身若不及之意，此作盡之。」
考試官右中允閔批：「婉曲有味。」
考試官侍讀華批：「詳贍明白。」

備官以爲周身之防，天子之禮也。蓋人君一身
translation_en:
…may not usurp the prerogatives of the Son of Heaven, and thus the ritual distinctions between superior and inferior are established. Thus, condemning their unauthorized action, though done on behalf of Jin and Wei, teaches loyalty to all who serve as ministers under Heaven; condemning their insubordination, though done on behalf of Lu, teaches reverence to all who serve as ministers under Heaven. Earlier scholars said that the Spring and Autumn Annals elucidates distinctions of status and duty. Is this not indeed true? Yet let us set aside reproaching the two ministers. Lu upheld the rites of Zhou, but could not set forth the great principles of right conduct to rebuff them. How weak it was! The Commentary states that when the two ministers were about to renew the covenant, the duke was uncertain about their order of precedence. Zang Xuanshu thereupon consulted ancient institutions in replying. His explanation was discriminating; yet on the point that regional lords and their ministers could not join together in the same covenant, he ultimately said not a word. Attentive to details but blind to the fundamental principles—how profoundly he failed to understand what mattered! Alas, I cannot but regret the conduct of Lu’s ruler and ministers.

Record of Rites (Liji)
“When he acts, the Scribe of the Left records it; when he speaks, the Scribe of the Right records it. The blind musicians attending him scrutinize the high and low tones of his voice.”
Cao Sanyang
Associate Examiner Zhou, School Instructor, comments: “This composition fully expresses the idea that a king examines his own conduct as though he could never do so adequately.”
Examiner Min, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: “Subtle and nuanced, with depth of meaning.”
Examiner Hua, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Full, ample, and clear.”

To provide a full complement of officials as safeguards encompassing one’s person is the ritual practice of the Son of Heaven. For the ruler’s own person…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
萬化之本也則夫備官以周其防者豈容巳哉
玉藻記天子之禮如此且天子者天下之表也
敬肆之間治忽繫焉固不可以不慎也然修之
雖存乎已而所以防之者不能不賴乎人是故
自出入起居以至賞罰用舍天子不能無動也
動而弗書則以動莫予制而不幾於過則乎故
載筆而侍於其左者有左史焉史在於左所以
紀其動也不動則巳動則無不書之發乎邇而
見乎逺者將美惡之具陳也而所以慎其動者
===
弗能巳矣自命令訓辭以至詢謀論議天子不
能無言也言而弗書則以言莫予違而不幾於
過辭乎故載筆而侍於其右者有右史焉史在
於右所以紀其言也不言則巳言則無不書之
出乎身而加乎民者將是非之具見也而所以
慎其言者弗能巳矣乃若自閨門燕息以至朝
廷郊廟天子不能以無樂而樂之道與政通者
也不有以幾之則以政莫予議而肆焉以任情
者有矣故典樂而侍御者有工瞽焉工瞽之設
