punctuated: 萬化之本也，則夫備官以周其防者，豈容巳哉？《玉藻》記天子之禮如此。且天子者，天下之表也，敬肆之間，治忽繫焉，固不可以不慎也。然修之雖存乎已，而所以防之者，不能不賴乎人。是故自出入起居，以至賞罰用舍，天子不能無動也。動而弗書，則以動莫予制，而不幾於過則乎？故載筆而侍於其左者，有左史焉。史在於左，所以紀其動也。不動則巳，動則無不書之。發乎邇而見乎逺者，將美惡之具陳也，而所以慎其動者，弗能巳矣。自命令訓辭，以至詢謀論議，天子不能無言也。言而弗書，則以言莫予違，而不幾於過辭乎？故載筆而侍於其右者，有右史焉。史在於右，所以紀其言也。不言則巳，言則無不書之。出乎身而加乎民者，將是非之具見也，而所以慎其言者，弗能巳矣。乃若自閨門燕息，以至朝廷郊廟，天子不能以無樂，而樂之道，與政通者也。不有以幾之，則以政莫予議，而肆焉以任情者有矣。故典樂而侍御者，有工瞽焉。工瞽之設
translation_en:
…is the foundation of all transformation. How, then, could appointing a full complement of officials to provide comprehensive safeguards for him ever be dispensed with? The “Jade Bead Pendants” (Yuzao) chapter records the rites of the Son of Heaven in this way. Moreover, the Son of Heaven is the exemplar for all under Heaven. Order and disorder hinge upon whether he is reverent or unrestrained; he must therefore exercise care. Yet although self-cultivation rests with himself, the means of safeguarding him necessarily depend upon others.

Thus, from his comings and goings and daily activities to his bestowal of rewards and punishments and his employment or dismissal of men, the Son of Heaven cannot be without actions. If he acts and his actions are not recorded, will he not come close to transgressing proper standards, thinking, “No one restrains my actions”? Hence there is a Recorder of the Left, who attends at his left with writing brush in hand. The recorder is stationed on the left to record his actions. If he does not act, there is nothing to record; whenever he acts, nothing goes unrecorded. What originates close at hand and becomes manifest far away will have its good and bad aspects fully set forth. He thus cannot cease to exercise care in his actions.

From commands and admonitions to consultations and deliberations, the Son of Heaven cannot be without words. If he speaks and his words are not recorded, will he not come close to speaking improperly, thinking, “No one contradicts my words”? Hence there is a Recorder of the Right, who attends at his right with writing brush in hand. The recorder is stationed on the right to record his words. If he does not speak, there is nothing to record; whenever he speaks, nothing goes unrecorded. What issues from his person and affects the people will have its right and wrong aspects fully revealed. He thus cannot cease to exercise care in his words.

As for occasions ranging from repose in his private apartments to ceremonies at court, at the suburban altars, and in the ancestral temple, the Son of Heaven cannot dispense with music. The principles of music are interconnected with government. Without some means of examining it, he may think, “No one criticizes my government,” and give himself free rein, indulging his inclinations. Hence there are blind musicians who oversee music and attend upon him. The establishment of these blind musicians…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
所以幾其聲也其政和者其聲安以樂其政乖
者其聲怨以怒即其聲音之間察其高下之節
而政之施於天下者或得或失居然其可知矣
所以致樂以治心而修政以圖治者又焉能以
弗慎乎夫知動之必書而慎焉動爲道矣知言
之必書而慎焉言爲則矣知聲之必幾而慎焉
聲爲律矣天子檢身之道其嚴矣哉嗟夫此制
作之本也身之言動禮之謂也聲之上下樂之
謂也先王有史書之箴者防非僻之干履中正
也有工瞽之誦者防乖戾之漸樂和平也同民
心而出治道舉而措之無難矣故曰天子建中
和之極
揖讓而治天下者禮樂之謂也
周應祥
同考試官學正周批立意平正而詞復
雅馴蓋有得於揖讓之道者

考試官侍讀華批明暢

考試官右中允閔 批 〔充蔚可嘉〕
考試官侍讀華 批 〔明暢〕
punctuated:
所以幾其聲也。其政和者，其聲安以樂；其政乖者，其聲怨以怒。即其聲音之間，察其高下之節，而政之施於天下者，或得或失，居然其可知矣。所以致樂以治心，而修政以圖治者，又焉能以弗慎乎？夫知動之必書而慎焉，動爲道矣；知言之必書而慎焉，言爲則矣；知聲之必幾而慎焉，聲爲律矣。天子檢身之道，其嚴矣哉！嗟夫！此制作之本也。身之言動，禮之謂也；聲之上下，樂之謂也。先王有史書之箴者，防非僻之干，履中正也；有工瞽之誦者，防乖戾之漸，樂和平也。同民心而出治道，舉而措之，無難矣。故曰：「天子建中和之極。」

揖讓而治天下者，禮樂之謂也。
周應祥
同考試官學正周批：「立意平正，而詞復雅馴，蓋有得於揖讓之道者。」
考試官右中允閔批：「充蔚可嘉。」
考試官侍讀華批：「明暢。」
translation_en:
…serves to scrutinize his music. When his government is harmonious, its sounds are peaceful and joyful; when his government is discordant, its sounds are resentful and angry. By examining the modulation of high and low notes in that music, one can readily discern the successes and failures of government throughout the realm. How, then, could he fail to exercise care in perfecting music to govern his heart and reforming government to achieve good order? Knowing that his actions must be recorded and therefore exercising care, he makes his actions accord with the Way. Knowing that his words must be recorded and therefore exercising care, he makes his words a standard. Knowing that his music must be scrutinized and therefore exercising care, he makes its sounds conform to the pitch standards. How rigorous is the Son of Heaven’s discipline of himself! Ah! This is the foundation for establishing rites and music. The words and actions of the person are what is meant by ritual; the rising and falling of sounds are what is meant by music. The former kings had admonitions in the historians’ records to guard against the intrusion of wrongdoing and perversity and to walk in centrality and rectitude. They had recitations by the blind musicians to guard against the beginnings of discord and to delight in peace and harmony. By bringing the people’s hearts into accord and issuing the principles of good government, they could put these into practice without difficulty. Thus it is said: “The Son of Heaven establishes the supreme standard of centrality and harmony.”

“To govern all under Heaven through bowing and yielding: this is what is meant by rites and music.”
By Zhou Yingxiang.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, School Instructor: “The conception is balanced and correct, and the language is also elegant and refined. He seems to have grasped something of the Way of bowing and yielding.”

Comment by Examiner Min, Right Mentor: “Rich and flourishing; worthy of praise.”

Comment by Examiner Hua, Reader-in-waiting: “Clear and fluent.”

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
記者舉聖世無為之化而歸諸制作之極功焉
夫致禮樂之道則無為而天下化矣非古之聖
人其孰能與於斯記者論禮樂之至則無怨爭
而徵諸古如此以為天下至大也治天下至難
也固有竭心思之力而未得夫小康之效者况
可揖讓而治乎乃若古之聖人元首股肱揖遜
於殿陛而已矣未嘗見其作為之勞也而自成
風動之休都俞吁咈雍容於廟堂而已矣未嘗
覩其經綸之迹也而坐致時雍之盛化隆俗美
===
而四海各安其分蓋不疾而速也不行而至也
治道沛乎其莫禦矣風移俗易而萬物各得其
所蓋不見而章也不動而變也治功巍乎其有
成矣若此者豈大順大化之妙徒在於揖讓之
間哉亦由體信達順之方有得於禮樂之用耳
何則制作之道本諸身則建諸天地而不悖中
和之極立於上則達之天下而同歸故大禮之
制與天地而同序也聖人致禮之道則以序召
序而民咸納於規矩準繩之中彝倫攸敘秩秩

punctuated:
記者舉聖世無為之化，而歸諸制作之極功焉。
夫致禮樂之道，則無為而天下化矣。非古之聖人，其孰能與於斯？記者論禮樂之至，則無怨爭，而徵諸古如此。以為天下至大也，治天下至難也，固有竭心思之力而未得夫小康之效者，况可揖讓而治乎？乃若古之聖人，元首股肱揖遜於殿陛而已矣，未嘗見其作為之勞也，而自成風動之休；都俞吁咈，雍容於廟堂而已矣，未嘗覩其經綸之迹也，而坐致時雍之盛。化隆俗美，而四海各安其分，蓋不疾而速也，不行而至也，治道沛乎其莫禦矣；風移俗易，而萬物各得其所，蓋不見而章也，不動而變也，治功巍乎其有成矣。若此者，豈大順大化之妙徒在於揖讓之間哉？亦由體信達順之方，有得於禮樂之用耳。
何則？制作之道本諸身，則建諸天地而不悖；中和之極立於上，則達之天下而同歸。故大禮之制，與天地而同序也。聖人致禮之道，則以序召序，而民咸納於規矩準繩之中，彝倫攸敘，秩秩
translation_en:
The author of the Record invokes the transforming influence of an age of sages, achieved without action, and attributes it to the supreme accomplishment of establishing rites and music.
When the Way of rites and music is fully realized, all under Heaven are transformed without action. Who but the sages of antiquity could attain this? In discussing the perfection of rites and music, the author of the Record says that there is then neither resentment nor contention, and adduces antiquity as evidence in this manner. All under Heaven is vast indeed, and governing it is exceedingly difficult. There have certainly been those who exhausted their powers of thought without attaining even the results of modest peace and order. How, then, could one govern merely through bows and gestures of deference? Yet with the sages of antiquity, the sovereign and his ministers—the head and the limbs—merely bowed and yielded to one another at the palace steps. No toil of active intervention was ever apparent, yet the admirable effect of influence spreading like the wind arose of itself. They merely exchanged words of approval and dissent with dignified ease at court. No trace of their ordering and administering affairs was ever visible, yet without exertion they brought about the flourishing harmony of the age. Their transforming influence was profound and customs were fine, and everyone within the Four Seas rested content in their allotted station. They were swift without haste and arrived without travelling: the Way of government flowed abundantly, beyond all obstruction. Prevailing practices changed and customs were transformed, and all things found their proper places. It was manifest without being seen and brought change without movement: the achievement of government stood lofty and complete. Could the marvel of such perfect accord and transformation lie solely in bows and gestures of deference? It arose also from grasping the operation of rites and music through the method of embodying trustworthiness and extending accord.
Why is this so? When the Way of establishing institutions is rooted in one's own person, it can be set before Heaven and Earth without contradiction. When the highest standard of equilibrium and harmony is established above, it reaches all under Heaven, and all converge upon it. Thus the institutions of the great rites share the order of Heaven and Earth. When the sage fully realizes the Way of ritual, he uses order to summon order, bringing all the people within the compass, square, level, and marking line of proper conduct. The enduring human relationships are duly ordered, in orderly array…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
然自安其分而無所爭矣揖讓而治者非此禮
至之謂哉大樂之作與天地而同和也聖人致
樂之道則以和召和而民皆囿於欣喜歡愛之

translation_en:
…contentedly accepting their allotted stations, with nothing over which to contend. Is this not what is meant by ritual reaching its perfection, so that one governs through bows and deference? The creation of great music shares the harmony of Heaven and Earth. In bringing music to perfection, the sage summons harmony through harmony, so that all the people dwell amid joy, delight, affection, and love. Harmonious influences circulate everywhere; happily content in their places, they have nothing to resent. Is this not what is meant by music reaching its perfection, so that one governs through bows and deference?

Viewed in this light, vast though the realm may be, ritual and music are more than sufficient to guide it; difficult though achieving good government may be, grounding it in ritual and music makes the task manageable. Is this not why the government of the sages was so flourishing, beyond what later ages could attain? Moreover, among those who established ritual and music from antiquity onward, none surpassed the Duke of Zhou. Yet when the Duke of Zhou assisted King Cheng, he repeatedly and earnestly admonished him against ease. Combining the practices of the Three Kings and carrying out the four measures, he had no leisure by day or night. Was governing through bows and deference, then, merely an empty phrase? Not daring to take one's ease expresses the sage's determination to achieve good government; governing through bows and deference is the culmination of the sage's achievements and transforming influence. At the outset, the labor is indeed very great, but in the end the ease is very great. Would it not therefore be difficult to abandon the path of diligence and still seek government through bows and deference?

子之際矣
聖人之心其以天自處乎是故曠世而相為感
也夫周公聖人也達而在上孔子亦聖人也窮
而在下若不能以相及矣而聖人則以道之所
在天之所在自任之重不以窮達而有異焉是
故周公往矣而其道之未墜者孔子則欲舉而
行之以挽斯世於成周之盛終其身有不能一

translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: The conception is expansive and grand, the thought refined and enduring. Through more than a thousand flowing words, every movement of control and release, opening and closing, accords with proper measure; and Kongzi’s resolve to put the Way into practice overflows beyond the words. One may indeed call it a single voice leading and three voices responding, with resonance lingering afterward.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liang, Instructor: This discourse neither indulges in unrestrained flights nor labors over minute refinements. Yet its conception and phrasing are beyond the reach of an immature writer. Might he too aspire to the Way of the Duke of Zhou?

Comment by Examiner Min, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent: Arguments emerge one after another, their implications inexhaustible. Could such a work really have been produced in the examination hall!

Comment by Examiner Hua, Reader-in-Waiting: The meaning conveyed is deeply moving. This writer is someone with whom one can discuss the connection between the Duke of Zhou and Kongzi.

Does the sage’s heart not take Heaven as its own charge? Thus sages move one another even across distant ages. The Duke of Zhou was a sage who attained office and occupied a high position; Kongzi was also a sage, but was frustrated in his aspirations and remained below. It would seem that they could not reach one another. Yet the sage regards himself as the place where the Way resides and where Heaven resides; the weight of the responsibility he assumes does not differ according to whether his circumstances are adverse or favorable. Thus, although the Duke of Zhou had passed away, Kongzi wished to take up and put into practice the Way of his that had not fallen into oblivion, restoring the world to the flourishing condition of the established Zhou order. Throughout his life, he could not put this out of his heart for even a single day. What sort of heart is the sage’s heart? It is simply that, because the Way of Heaven resides in him, he cannot permit himself to evade his responsibility. Ah! This is why Kongzi, in relation to the Duke of Zhou…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
曠世而相感也歟今夫天之生斯民也不能自
治必生聖人焉而以斯道畀之聖人者道之所
寄而代天以終其事者也斯道之傳由孔子而
上可考而知也孔子固嘗祖述堯舜矣憲章文
武矣又曰行夏時乘殷輅矣至其夢寐所感獨
於周公乎見之何哉蓋聖人之道未嘗不同而
時之所值不能無異道之行也亦隨其時而已
矣是故其在伊尹也樂堯舜之道焉堯舜而上
非無聖人也而去伊尹則遠矣其在周公也思
===
兼三王之道焉三王而上非無聖人也而去周
公則遠矣夫周公之志猶伊尹也而孔子之志
獨異於周公乎況夫堯舜之道傳之三王而周
公則兼之其所以相成王治天下者經之綸之
綱之紀之若設官分職辨方正位體國經野博
大纖悉靡不畢具故一時教化大行刑措不用
行葦歌其忠厚旣醉嘉其太平而三代之禮至
是而大備是堯舜三王之道統會於周公而行

punctuated: 曠世而相感也歟？今夫天之生斯民也，不能自治，必生聖人焉，而以斯道畀之。聖人者，道之所寄，而代天以終其事者也。斯道之傳，由孔子而上，可考而知也。孔子固嘗祖述堯舜矣，憲章文武矣，又曰行夏時、乘殷輅矣。至其夢寐所感，獨於周公乎見之，何哉？蓋聖人之道未嘗不同，而時之所值不能無異，道之行也，亦隨其時而已矣。是故其在伊尹也，樂堯舜之道焉。堯舜而上，非無聖人也，而去伊尹則遠矣。其在周公也，思兼三王之道焉。三王而上，非無聖人也，而去周公則遠矣。夫周公之志，猶伊尹也，而孔子之志，獨異於周公乎？況夫堯舜之道，傳之三王，而周公則兼之。其所以相成王治天下者，經之綸之，綱之紀之，若設官分職、辨方正位、體國經野，博大纖悉，靡不畢具。故一時教化大行，刑措不用，《行葦》歌其忠厚，《旣醉》嘉其太平，而三代之禮至是而大備。是堯舜三王之道，統會於周公，而行周公之道者，即所以行堯舜三王之道也。且堯
translation_en:
…responded to one another across the ages, was it not? Now, when Heaven gives birth to these people, they cannot govern themselves; it must therefore bring forth sages and entrust this Way to them. Sages are those in whom the Way resides, who act on Heaven’s behalf to complete its work. The transmission of this Way can be traced and understood by looking back from Kongzi. Kongzi indeed carried forward the teachings of Yao and Shun and took Wen and Wu as his models. He also spoke of following the Xia calendar and riding in the Yin carriage. Yet the inspiration that came to him in his dreams appeared in Zhougong alone. Why was this? The Way of the sages has never differed, but the circumstances of their times necessarily vary; the practice of the Way simply accords with its time.

Thus Yi Yin delighted in the Way of Yao and Shun. There had certainly been sages before Yao and Shun, but they were remote from Yi Yin. Zhougong sought to unite the Ways of the Three Kings. There had certainly been sages before the Three Kings, but they were remote from Zhougong. Zhougong’s aspiration was like Yi Yin’s: could Kongzi’s aspiration alone have differed from Zhougong’s? Moreover, the Way of Yao and Shun was transmitted to the Three Kings, and Zhougong brought it all together. In assisting King Cheng to govern all under Heaven, he ordered and arranged affairs, establishing their guiding principles and detailed regulations. Such matters as establishing offices and dividing responsibilities, distinguishing directions and setting positions correctly, laying out the capital and demarcating the countryside—everything, from the broadest scope to the finest detail, was fully provided for. Thus moral instruction spread widely in his time, and punishments were set aside and left unused. The poem Spreading Reeds (Xing wei) celebrated its loyal generosity, and Already Drunk (Ji zui) praised its great peace; the rites of the Three Dynasties thereby reached their fullest development. Thus the Way of Yao, Shun, and the Three Kings was united in Zhougong, and to practice Zhougong’s Way was precisely to practice theirs. Furthermore, Yao…

誰與歸故曰周監於二代郁郁乎文哉吾從周
夫文者道之顯者也周公之文文之至也周公
既沒道不在孔子乎故曰天之將喪斯文也後
死者不得與於斯文也天之未喪斯文也匡人
其如予何蓋孔子以天自處有不可得而辭者
矣孔子之時何時也周室東遷黍離既降文武
之政不及於天下久矣苟有周公者出而相焉
布在方策者猶可舉也而若宰咺祭伯祭公渠

translation_en:
…Shun and the Three Kings were sovereigns; the Duke of Zhou was a minister, and Confucius too was a minister. Whom could he follow if he abandoned the Duke of Zhou? Thus he said: “Zhou took the two preceding dynasties as its models. How splendid its cultural refinement! I follow Zhou.” Cultural refinement is the visible manifestation of the Way. The cultural refinement of the Duke of Zhou was its highest realization. Once the Duke of Zhou had died, did the Way not reside in Confucius? Thus he said: “Had Heaven intended to destroy this culture, I, who came after, would not have been able to share in it. Since Heaven has not destroyed this culture, what can the people of Kuang do to me?” Confucius thus understood his position in terms of Heaven’s charge: there was a responsibility he could not decline.

What sort of age was the age of Confucius? The Zhou royal house had moved east, and “Millet Droops” had already been relegated to a lower category in the Book of Odes. The government of Kings Wen and Wu had long ceased to reach all under Heaven. Had someone like the Duke of Zhou emerged to serve as chief minister, the institutions recorded in the texts could still have been put into practice. Yet men such as Zai Xuan, the Earl of Zhai, the Duke of Zhai, and the Earl of Qu all occupied positions like that of the Duke of Zhou, but personally took the lead in violating laws and disrupting order. If one hoped that the subordinate states would follow their example and be transformed, who would stand with us? Thus Qi instituted its internal administration, Jin instituted yuanju [?], and Zheng established field boundaries and irrigation ditches and cast its penal statutes in metal. I find no fault with the means by which men such as Guan Zhong and Zichan assisted their rulers. But Lu, through its military levies on qiu land units and its taxation by the mu, likewise imitated the bad precedents of the other states. What can one say of this? Confucius truly could not bear to see the rites of Zhou collapse overnight. Thus he said: “When the Way prevails under Heaven, rites, music, and punitive expeditions issue from the Son of Heaven.” Were his expectations of the Eastern Zhou ruler not exceedingly high? Why was this? The Son of Heaven is the ruler of all under Heaven. Where that authority resides, the Way can readily be put into practice. If only he could find a ruler like King Cheng and serve as his chief minister, the good government of Chengzhou would again appear throughout the realm, and…

盡斬天之意猶在周也觀賢者不得志而思盛
際之顯王也則曰云誰之思西方美人大夫顧
瞻周道而弔於心也則曰誰將西歸懷之好音
小國困斃思撥亂以治也則曰愾我寤嘆念彼
周京雖以秦風之武悍而驪山之役猶不失同
仇之誼則民心未始忘周而天意可知矣苟有
用我者吾將建之六官分之庶職疆之侯甸采
衛以定其域統之比閭族黨以屬其民疏之溝
洫涂澮以井其田制之伍兩卒旅以治其師通
之朝聘會同燕饗以協其情列之車旗圭璧服
物采章以辨其等凡周公之所已試者吾皆舉
而措之天下無難矣此固夫子之志所以惓惓
而不能自已者乎充斯志也寶玉大弓必不欲
其入於盜臣之手樹旅反坫必不欲其陳於大
夫之庭朱干玉戚雉門兩觀必不欲其設於諸
侯之國使禮樂征伐一出於天子而僭竊者不
得肆聖人憂世之心其少釋乎柰之何東周之

…I might then become a Duke of Zhou. Moreover, although the Way of Zhou had declined, the beneficent legacy of Kings Wen and Wu had not been wholly cut off: Heaven’s favor still rested with Zhou. Consider how worthy men, frustrated in their aspirations, longed for the illustrious kings of its flourishing age, saying: “Of whom do I think? Of that beautiful person in the west.” When great officers looked back upon the Way of Zhou and grieved in their hearts, they said: “Who will return westward? I would cherish good tidings from him.” When small states were exhausted by hardship and longed for disorder to be quelled and good government restored, they said: “Ah, waking, I sigh, thinking of that Zhou capital.” Even with the martial fierceness expressed in the Airs of Qin, the campaign at Lishan still preserved the bond of facing a common enemy. Thus the people’s hearts had never forgotten Zhou, and Heaven’s intention can be understood.

If someone would employ me, I would establish the six ministries and distribute their various duties; delimit the hou, dian, cai, and wei domains to fix their territories; organize the people into bi, lü, zu, and dang neighborhood groupings to unite them; lay out ditches, channels, roads, and larger waterways to arrange their fields in the well-field system; establish units of five, twenty-five, one hundred, and five hundred men to order their armies; maintain communication through court audiences, diplomatic visits, assemblies, formal gatherings, and banquets to harmonize their sentiments; and prescribe graded chariots, banners, jade tablets and disks, robes, articles of use, and colored insignia to distinguish their ranks. Everything that the Duke of Zhou had already put into practice I would adopt and implement: there would be no difficulty in governing all under Heaven. Surely this explains why the Master cherished his aspiration so earnestly and could not relinquish it!

To fulfill this aspiration, he would certainly not wish precious jade and the great bow to fall into the hands of thieving ministers, nor “erected screens” [?] and stands for returning drinking cups to be displayed in the courtyards of great officers, nor vermilion shields and jade axes, the Pheasant Gate and its paired towers to be installed in the states of the feudal lords. If rites, music, punitive expeditions, and warfare all proceeded solely from the Son of Heaven, and those who usurped authority could no longer act unchecked, might the sage’s concern for the world be somewhat eased? text:
君不足與有為於是退而欲試於魯焉自其宰
中都以至攝相事羔豚不飾價男女别於途一
變至道蓋已微露其機而歸侵田却萊夷墮三
都誅少正卯居然周公之典刑也當是時兆足
以行矣未幾而女樂之饋卒以沮之及其告老
也聞陳恒之變猶沐浴而請討蓋欲以天子之
權與周公之後而魯之君臣又不能盡如其意
於是正名則欲行諸衛君君臣臣父父子子則
欲行諸齊甚者公山佛肸之召亦欲往焉至於
===
轍環天下雖削迹而不避見厄而不沮取譏於
荷蕢丈人之徒而不恤其心何若是急乎誠以
周公之道不可一日不行於天下也周流列國
蓋庶幾一遇焉而卒未得也於是歸與之思作
而行道之志窮矣雖然孔子亦安能遂忘周公
哉周公之道具載周禮而周禮之在魯也則君
子嘗因易象春秋而知之矣故取易象而贊之

修之繫王於天而予以天命貶以天討謂足以

君不足與有為，於是退而欲試於魯焉。自其宰中都，以至攝相事，羔豚不飾價，男女别於途，一變至道，蓋已微露其機。而歸侵田，却萊夷，墮三都，誅少正卯，居然周公之典刑也。當是時，兆足以行矣。未幾而女樂之饋，卒以沮之。及其告老也，聞陳恒之變，猶沐浴而請討，蓋欲以天子之權與周公之後，而魯之君臣又不能盡如其意。於是正名則欲行諸衛，君君、臣臣、父父、子子則欲行諸齊。甚者，公山、佛肸之召，亦欲往焉。至於轍環天下，雖削迹而不避，見厄而不沮，取譏於荷蕢、丈人之徒而不恤，其心何若是急乎？誠以周公之道不可一日不行於天下也。周流列國，蓋庶幾一遇焉，而卒未得也。於是歸與之思作，而行道之志窮矣。

雖然，孔子亦安能遂忘周公哉？周公之道具載周禮，而周禮之在魯也，則君子嘗因易象、春秋而知之矣。故取易象而贊之，謂足以明天道矣；見諸行事，則未也。取春秋而修之，繫王於天，而予以天命，貶以天討，謂足以

…the ruler was inadequate as a partner in accomplishing anything, so Confucius withdrew and sought to put his principles into practice in Lu. From his service as magistrate of Zhongdu through his acting service as chief minister, sellers did not inflate the prices of lambs and pigs, and men and women kept to separate paths. With a single transformation, Lu could attain the Way: the beginnings of this possibility were already faintly apparent. Securing the return of encroached-upon lands, repelling the Lai tribesmen, demolishing the fortifications of the three cities, and executing Shaozheng Mao—all these unmistakably embodied the exemplary institutions of the Duke of Zhou. At that time, the initial signs suggested that the Way could be put into practice [?]. Before long, however, the gift of female musicians ultimately frustrated his efforts. Even after he had retired, when he heard of Chen Heng’s act of regicide, he still bathed and requested a punitive expedition. His intention was to place the authority of the Son of Heaven in the hands of the Duke of Zhou’s descendant; yet the ruler and ministers of Lu again failed to fulfill his wishes entirely. Thus he wished to carry out the rectification of names in Wei, and to establish in Qi the principle that rulers should act as rulers, ministers as ministers, fathers as fathers, and sons as sons. He went so far as to wish to accept even the summonses of Gongshan and Bi Xi. He traveled throughout the realm in his carriage; though his tracks were effaced, he did not turn aside, and though he encountered adversity, he was not discouraged. Nor did he concern himself with the ridicule of such men as the basket carrier and the old man. Why was his heart so urgent? Truly, it was because the Way of the Duke of Zhou could not be left unpracticed in the world for even a single day. He traveled among the various states, hoping perhaps to encounter just one ruler who would receive him, but in the end he found none. Then the thought, “Let me return!” arose, and his ambition to put the Way into practice reached an impasse.

Even so, how could Confucius ever forget the Duke of Zhou? The Duke of Zhou’s Way is fully recorded in the Rites of Zhou; and that the rites of Zhou survived in Lu was something the gentleman had already learned through the Images of the Changes and the Spring and Autumn Annals. Thus Confucius took the Images of the Changes and composed elucidations of them, considering these sufficient to illuminate the Way of Heaven. Yet they did not embody it in actual deeds. title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
紹周公之志矣而猶未也敘國風也終豳風之
什考尚書也錄文侯之命夫曹檜之後去豳風
遠矣亂極思治故以豳風終焉思周公也文侯
之功其去周公又遠矣而迹則似之思周公而
不見見似周公者猶有取焉其寤寐周公之志
蓋隨感而輒見也及其衰也已無復可覬矣而
猶有不夢之嘆焉誠有一息尚存此志不容少
懈者矣於乎此其心之相感豈世之先後身之
窮達所得而拘耶大抵聖人之道一而已矣周
===
公在上而道行孔子在下而道不行固有易地
皆然者周公之幸而不為孔子與孔子之不幸
而不為周公皆天也聖人何容心哉繼孔子者
有孟子焉以王政勸齊梁之君而井田學校告
文公者惓惓不置其欲行孔子之道猶孔子之
於周公也故嘗自信以為天欲平治天下舍我
其誰而其敘道統之傳曰然而無有乎爾則亦
無有乎爾此其以天自處亦有不可得而辭者
乎是故知孟子之志則孔子之志益可見矣

punctuated: 紹周公之志矣，而猶未也。敘國風也，終豳風之什；考尚書也，錄文侯之命。夫曹檜之後，去豳風遠矣。亂極思治，故以豳風終焉，思周公也。文侯之功，其去周公又遠矣，而迹則似之。思周公而不見，見似周公者，猶有取焉。其寤寐周公之志，蓋隨感而輒見也。及其衰也，已無復可覬矣，而猶有不夢之嘆焉。誠有一息尚存，此志不容少懈者矣。於乎！此其心之相感，豈世之先後、身之窮達所得而拘耶？大抵聖人之道，一而已矣。周公在上而道行，孔子在下而道不行，固有易地皆然者。周公之幸而不為孔子，與孔子之不幸而不為周公，皆天也。聖人何容心哉？繼孔子者，有孟子焉。以王政勸齊梁之君，而井田學校告文公者，惓惓不置。其欲行孔子之道，猶孔子之於周公也。故嘗自信以為：「天欲平治天下，舍我其誰？」而其敘道統之傳曰：「然而無有乎爾，則亦無有乎爾。」此其以天自處，亦有不可得而辭者乎？是故知孟子之志，則孔子之志益可見矣。
translation_en:
…carry on the aspirations of the Duke of Zhou, yet even this was not enough. In arranging the Airs of the States, Confucius placed the Airs of Bin last; in examining the Book of Documents, he included the Charge to Marquis Wen. The age represented by the Airs of Cao and Kuai was far removed from that of the Airs of Bin. When disorder reaches its extreme, one longs for good government; thus he concluded with the Airs of Bin, out of longing for the Duke of Zhou. Marquis Wen’s achievements, too, fell far short of those of the Duke of Zhou, yet his deeds resembled the duke’s. Longing for the Duke of Zhou but unable to see him, Confucius still found something worthy of inclusion when he encountered someone who resembled him. His constant devotion to the Duke of Zhou, waking and sleeping, thus manifested itself whenever something stirred his feelings. When he grew old, there was no longer anything he could hope for, yet he still lamented that he no longer dreamed of the duke. Truly, so long as a single breath remained, he could not allow this aspiration to slacken even slightly. Alas! How could this communion of their hearts be constrained by the different ages in which they lived, or by whether their own circumstances were straitened or prosperous? The Way of the sages is, after all, one and the same. The Duke of Zhou occupied a high position, and his Way was put into practice; Confucius occupied a low position, and his Way was not. Had they exchanged places, each would surely have acted as the other did. That the Duke of Zhou was fortunate and did not share Confucius’s lot, and that Confucius was unfortunate and did not share the Duke of Zhou’s lot, were both Heaven’s doing. What room was there for the sages’ personal wishes?

Confucius’s successor was Mengzi. He urged the rulers of Qi and Liang to practice kingly government, and tirelessly instructed Duke Wen concerning the well-field system and schools. His desire to put Confucius’s Way into practice was like Confucius’s devotion to the Duke of Zhou. Thus he once declared with confidence: “If Heaven wishes to bring peace and order to the world, who but me could do it?” In recounting the transmission of the succession of the Way, he said: “Yet there is no one now; then there will be no one hereafter.” In thus understanding his own position in relation to Heaven, did he not also acknowledge a responsibility he could not decline? Therefore, once we understand Mengzi’s aspirations, those of Confucius become still clearer.

…the martial might of Shang undertook a three-year campaign. Against the unruly Xianyun, the armies of Zhou labored on the expedition celebrated in “The Sixth Month.” From Qin and Han onward, defiance grew ever greater. Lofty walls were built along the northern frontier, merely ravaging the veins of the earth; an ingenious stratagem was deployed at Baideng, only diminishing the state’s prestige. Gold and silk sent to the great desert increased year after year, while warning beacons repeatedly flared at Ganquan. When the reign of Jianyuan arrived, anger found expression in unrestrained warfare. Though victories were won, the toil and expense roughly matched the gains. Never had all the hundred barbarian peoples offered their treasures and looked up to the One Man, acknowledging him as their supreme center.
Now, however, we have humbly encountered Your Majesty, whose outstanding talent surpasses all others and whose sagacious strategies approach the divine. First you took up the vermilion banner and gloriously established your achievement at Jinyang; then you again wielded the yellow battle-axe and won great victories in the passes and the northern lands. You captured Jieli and laid waste his court, sweeping away the accumulated mists of Yinshan; you took heads at Gaochang to anoint the war drums with blood, clearing the enduring current of the Ruoshui. Displayed in the purple halls and vermilion chambers, it will sufficiently demonstrate that none lie beyond the reach of the celestial court; preserved in golden coffers and stone chambers, it may provide evidence for the dynastic history. Dou Xian erected an inscribed stele, yet his achievements were celebrated only north of the desert; Ma Yuan erected pillars, yet his awesome reputation shook only southern Dian. This magnificent creation embodies a benevolence like that of Heaven and Earth, nurturing all things!

…Your exposition is thorough and complete, and its abundant loyalty and devotion are palpable. Are you merely someone who probes the Classics and investigates antiquity? We have high hopes for you when you appear to answer before the imperial court.
The sage king reveres Heaven through substance rather than outward form, and models himself on his ancestors through their intentions rather than their outward deeds. Heaven is not remote from the ruler: its great mandate passes between them. Ancestors are not remote from their descendants: the same virtue links those who came before with those who follow. Thus, revering Heaven does not consist merely in grandly burning sacrificial firewood and presenting animals and silk to fulfill the outward forms. One must truly take Heaven’s discernment as one’s model, so as to stand worthily before it without disgrace. Modeling oneself on one’s ancestors does not consist merely in ascending the imperial throne and maintaining established standards to follow their outward deeds. One must have the resolve to seek and carry forward the virtue of preceding generations, so as to requite and extol it without departing from it. Such undertakings as the sacrifices at the Tai Altar at Ganquan ultimately became encumbered by excessive desires; the feng sacrifices in the east and offerings in the west could not avoid profaning the spirits. This was to embellish empty forms while lacking substantive governance, far removed from the Way of Heaven. Those who scrupulously preserved institutions nevertheless mixed disparate principles in their governance; those who practiced benevolence and generosity nevertheless declined in military achievement. This was to cling to ancient precedents while failing to understand what the times required, far removed from ancestral virtue. How could such conduct qualify as revering Heaven and modeling oneself on one’s ancestors?

…in a renewed creation, raising the sun and moon to shine anew: how lofty was his achievement in taking Heaven as his model! I humbly observe that, at the beginning of his reign, when announcing his accession through sacrifice at the Southern Suburb, he admonished the officials charged with conducting the rites, saying: “A person attends upon the Lord on High with a single heart. If there is the slightest insincerity, negligence will surely seize its opportunity; if reverence lapses for an instant, selfish desires will surely enter through the opening. What moves Heaven and Earth and touches the spirits is sincerity and reverence alone. Though Heaven is high, what it scrutinizes is very near; though the spirits are hidden, their presence is manifest. If one understands that the principle governing Heaven and humanity is one, one cannot permit the slightest neglect of sincerity and reverence in one’s heart.” These words embody the effort of keeping Heaven’s mandate constantly in view, the utmost attainment of sagely self-cultivation, and the foundation for receiving the mandate.

Thus the assisting minister Fu Huan praised him, saying: “Your Majesty cultivates virtue and examines your faults, with concern showing in your countenance. Though occupying an exalted position, you listen to those below; Heaven truly scrutinizes this.” Here the substance of reverence for Heaven was evidenced in his countenance. Song Lian praised him, saying: “His Majesty reveres and stands in awe of Heaven and Earth. In every movement and every moment of stillness, he is solemn, as though divine beings were above him.” Here the substance of reverence for Heaven resided in his heart. He also said: “Your Majesty models yourself on Heaven and inaugurates a new dynastic destiny, striving tirelessly throughout the day, without leisure even to eat.” Here the substance of reverence for Heaven appeared in his actions. What is meant by revering Heaven through substance rather than outward forms was already witnessed and understood by the ministers of that time. The Book of Documents says: “Heaven is difficult to rely upon; its mandate is not constant. Maintain constancy in your virtue, and preserve your position.” …

…The Sagely Founder possessed these qualities. Thus his brilliant virtue was expansive and great, readily beheld; his instructive words were coherent in principle, readily followed; his royal standards shone brightly, readily emulated; and his far-reaching plans were truly comprehensive, readily pursued. Are not the plans through which the former sage bequeathed his standards precisely the essentials that the later sage should take as his model? Our Emperor is endowed by Heaven with sagacity and discernment; his institutions combine the transmission of precedents with new creation. The three rites are all complete, and the hundred regulations are correct. He established the suburban sacrificial altars and ancestral temples to perform the highest ceremonies of the Three Dynasties, and erected the Hall of Enlightenment to revive the discontinued undertaking of the kings of successive ages. How magnificent are these rites of succession!
Recently, he reverently conferred the grand title “August Heaven, the Lord on High.” On the day celebrating the successful completion of the great sacrifice, he issued an imperial instruction to his assembled ministers, saying: “Knowing whom to revere, one honors the revered. In every word and every action, extending even to rewards and punishments, one dares not indulge one's own selfish desires. Knowing whom to hold dear, one cherishes one's kin. 日諸臣固已欽承之矣書曰至治馨香感
於神明黍稷非馨明德惟馨
皇上有焉故抑畏履盈慎德也丕承謨訓極孝
也緝熙光明基命也勑幾申戒交修也
punctuated: 父之道，是謂之天子。斯言也，昭事之原，宥密之學，而繼述之孝也。故遵《皇矣》之大訓，去昊天之偏名，定皇祖所未定也；曰「皇天」，以示尊尊之義，曰「上帝」，以示親親之義，發皇祖所未發也；祀皇祖於圜丘以配天，宗皇考於明堂以配帝，備皇祖所未備也。所謂法祖以心不以迹者，今日諸臣固已欽承之矣。《書》曰：「至治馨香，感於神明。黍稷非馨，明德惟馨。」皇上有焉。故抑畏履盈，愼德也；丕承謨訓，極孝也；緝熈光明，基命也；勅幾申戒，交修也。
translation_en:
…the way of serving one’s father: this is what it means to be the Son of Heaven. These words express the source of reverent service to Heaven, the learning of profound stillness, and the filial devotion that carries forward ancestral intentions and undertakings. Thus, by following the great admonition of the ode “August Indeed” (Huang yi) and abandoning the partial designation “Vast Heaven” (Haotian), His Majesty settled what his imperial ancestor had left unsettled. By using “August Heaven” (Huangtian) to express the duty of honoring the honored, and “Lord on High” (Shangdi) to express the duty of cherishing one’s kin, he brought forth what his imperial ancestor had not articulated. By sacrificing to his imperial ancestor at the Circular Mound as the correlate of Heaven, and honoring his deceased imperial father at the Hall of Light as the correlate of the Lord on High, he completed what his imperial ancestor had left incomplete. What is meant by following the ancestors in their intentions rather than their outward actions has certainly already been reverently received by all the ministers today.

The Book of Documents says: “The fragrance of consummate government reaches the spirits. It is not millet that is fragrant; only luminous virtue is fragrant.” His Majesty possesses this virtue. Thus, his humility and awe, proceeding as though carrying a brimming vessel, show his care for virtue; his magnificent continuation of ancestral counsels and instructions shows the utmost filial devotion; his sustained cultivation of brilliance and light establishes the foundation of the Mandate; and his vigilance over the first stirrings of affairs and repeated admonitions promote mutual cultivation.

translation_en:
…Is not this communion brought about by undivided virtue the foundation of divine protection and guidance for ten thousand generations? I have considered this: the government of a true king seeks its source in Heaven, while the art of succeeding to the throne takes the ancestors as its model. These are not two distinct ways. Thus only with Heaven’s virtue can one practice Heaven’s Way; only with the method of the heart can one perfect the methods of government. Extended to their fullest scope, these principles reach from the innermost palace to the great court: herein lies the means of ascending and descending in the presence of the spirits [?]. They extend from private leisure to the crucial affairs of government: herein lies the means of keeping the ancestors vividly present, never forgetting them.
When regulating expenditure and carefully observing limits, one says: “These are Heaven’s resources, bequeathed by my ancestors.” When lightening labor services and reducing taxes, one says: “These are Heaven’s people, cherished by my ancestors.” When establishing offices and appointing officials, one says: “This is Heaven’s work. Drawing near to worthy men and keeping petty men at a distance was how my ancestors made the dynasty flourish.” When bestowing rewards and wielding the authority to punish, one says: “These are Heaven’s commands and Heaven’s chastisements. Rewards must correspond to merit, and punishments must correspond to offenses: this was how my ancestors governed all under Heaven.” Only then will my heart be the heart of my ancestors, and Heaven’s Way be my way. 無夭扎，享靈長之祚，成光裕之業，人君之道斯其至矣。昔禹、益之陳謨也，言吉凶影響，而必曰罔失法度焉；傅說之納誨也，言奉若天道，而必曰允恊成德焉。其欲法祖以懋敬天之實乎？伊尹之作訓也，稱烈祖成德，而必曰上帝不常焉；周公之進戒也，稱太王、王季，而必曰克自抑畏焉。其欲敬天以成法祖之功乎？故以言其理，則一貫矣；以言其事，則相須矣。
今日在廷諸臣，固皆有禹、益、伊、傅、周公之責者，方共供相祀之職，奉宣諭之音，其必惕然而感，奮然而興乎？上下交而德業成，愚何幸身親見之！

translation_en:
…[the people] suffer no untimely death or pestilence [?], and the ruler enjoys enduring blessings and accomplishes the work of gloriously enriching his ancestral legacy. Here the Way of the ruler reaches its highest point. Long ago, when Yu and Yi presented their counsels, they spoke of good and ill fortune following like shadows and echoes, yet invariably said, “Do not depart from laws and standards.” When Fu Yue offered instruction, he spoke of reverently following the Way of Heaven, yet invariably said, “Truly accord with perfected virtue.” Did they wish to take the ancestors as models in order to deepen the substance of reverence for Heaven? When Yi Yin composed his instructions, he praised the illustrious ancestor’s perfected virtue, yet invariably said, “The Lord on High is not constant [in his favor].” When the Duke of Zhou offered admonitions, he praised King Tai and Wang Ji, yet invariably said, “They could restrain themselves and maintain reverent fear.” Did they wish to revere Heaven in order to accomplish the work of following the ancestors? Thus, considered in terms of principle, these are united by a single thread; considered in terms of practice, they depend upon one another.
The ministers now at court all bear responsibilities like those of Yu, Yi, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, and the Duke of Zhou. As they together discharge their duties of assisting at the sacrifices and receive the words of the imperial pronouncement, surely they will be moved to vigilance and stirred to action! When those above and below communicate, virtue and achievement are brought to completion. How fortunate I, in my humble station, am to witness this in person!

聖天子繼述之一助也
同考試官教諭陳　批　書史一策前代故
實與我
朝令典學者罕知子能因問條對而文斷以己意必有養之士
也
考試官右中允閔　批　此策於書史二者既隨事
敷陳而復取東先達之論識見卓邁不徒文之
佳而已也
===
考試官侍讀華　批　博古通今具見學識讀之
令人起敬
載千古之道存乎書書欲其備則典之者
貴得其人紀一代之事存乎史史欲其善
則作之者貴盡其職夫書以載道天下之
大經大法寓焉茍有未備則文獻無徵何
以考前王而不繆史以紀事天下之公是
公非繫焉茍有未善則勸懲無裨何以俟
後聖而不惑此所以典之者不可不得其
punctuated:
聖祖深致意焉。此策不惟具悉始末，而復各有以處之，眞可爲聖天子繼述之一助也。

同考試官教諭陳批：「書史一策，前代故實與我朝令典，學者罕知。子能因問條對，而又斷以己意，必有養之士也。」

考試官右中允閔批：「此策於書史二者，旣隨事敷陳，而後取衷先達之論，識見卓邁，不徒文之佳而已也。」

考試官侍讀華批：「博古通今，具見學識，讀之令人起敬。」

載千古之道存乎書，書欲其備，則典之者貴得其人；紀一代之事存乎史，史欲其善，則作之者貴盡其職。夫書以載道，天下之大經大法寓焉。苟有未備，則文獻無徵，何以考前王而不繆？史以紀事，天下之公是公非繫焉。苟有未善，則勸懲無裨，何以俟後聖而不惑？此所以典之者不可不得其
translation_en:
…the Sagely Progenitor gave these matters profound attention. This policy essay not only fully explains their history but also offers ways to address each of them. It can truly assist the sagely Son of Heaven in carrying forward his predecessor’s work.

Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor, comments: “As regards this policy question on books and histories, scholars seldom know the precedents of earlier dynasties and the excellent institutions of our own. You have answered the question point by point and have also offered judgments of your own. You must be a man of cultivated learning.”

Examiner Min, Right Mentor, comments: “In treating books and histories, this policy essay first expounds each matter and then seeks a balanced judgment in the discussions of earlier worthies. Its insight is outstanding; its excellence is by no means merely literary.”

Examiner Hua, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Thorough knowledge of antiquity and understanding of the present: learning and discernment are evident throughout. Reading it inspires respect.”

The transmission of the Way through the ages rests upon books. If books are to be complete, it is essential to find the right people to take charge of them. The recording of a dynasty’s affairs rests upon histories. If histories are to be well written, it is essential that those who compose them fully discharge their duties. Books convey the Way: within them reside the great norms and laws of all under Heaven. If they are incomplete, documentary and learned testimony cannot be verified; how, then, can one examine the former kings without error? Histories record events: upon them depend impartial judgments of right and wrong throughout the realm. If they are deficient, they offer no help in encouraging good and deterring evil; how, then, can one await a future sage without misgiving? This is why those who take charge of books must be the right…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
人而作之者不可不盡其職也我
聖祖之在當時固嘗留意於此而今日
聖天子繼述之孝豈容緩歟請因明問而敬陳
之古者内史掌邦國之志外史掌三皇五
帝之書國之圖籍各有司存至漢則藏書
之策建於武帝求書之詔下於孝成固世
之盛舉也其後若唐有四庫之目宋有三
館之儲雖所蓄未必皆精然其用意蒐輯
使千古之典籍賴以不墜亦可謂有功矣
===
古者左史紀動右史紀言事之美惡無不
備書至漢則西京之起居注設於禁廷東
都之起居注作於宮掖亦古之遺意也其
後若時政記則始於姚璹日曆則始於韋
執誼雖其意未必盡公然其及時紀錄使
一代之事蹟賴以不泯亦未為無補矣洪
惟我
聖祖開基當至元丙午之歲即下
令以求遺書及洪武癸丑之秋復

惟我
聖祖開基當至元丙午之歲即下
令以求遺書及洪武癸丑之秋復
punctuated:
人，而作之者不可不盡其職也。我聖祖之在當時，固嘗留意於此，而今日聖天子繼述之孝，豈容緩歟？請因明問而敬陳之。古者内史掌邦國之志，外史掌三皇五帝之書，國之圖籍各有司存。至漢，則藏書之策建於武帝，求書之詔下於孝成，固世之盛舉也。其後，若唐有四庫之目，宋有三館之儲，雖所蓄未必皆精，然其用意蒐輯，使千古之典籍賴以不墜，亦可謂有功矣。

古者左史紀動，右史紀言，事之美惡，無不備書。至漢，則西京之起居注設於禁廷，東都之起居注作於宮掖，亦古之遺意也。其後，若時政記則始於姚璹，日曆則始於韋執誼，雖其意未必盡公，然其及時紀錄，使一代之事蹟賴以不泯，亦未為無補矣。洪惟我聖祖開基，當至元丙午之歲，即下令以求遺書；及洪武癸丑之秋，復
translation_en:
…the right men, while those who compose histories must fully discharge their duties. Our Sagely Progenitor certainly devoted attention to this in his day. How, then, could our present Sagely Son of Heaven permit any delay in carrying forward his ancestor’s work with filial devotion? Allow me respectfully to set forth my views in response to your discerning question. In antiquity, the Inner Scribe managed the records of the states, and the Outer Scribe managed the writings of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors; the realm’s maps and documents each had their appointed custodians. Under the Han, a policy of collecting books was established by Emperor Wu, and an edict seeking books was issued by Emperor Xiaocheng. These were indeed great undertakings of their age. Subsequently, the Tang had the catalogue of the Four Repositories, and the Song had the collections of the Three Institutes. Although their holdings were not necessarily all of the highest quality, their deliberate efforts to seek out and collect books enabled the writings of the ages to survive. These efforts may indeed be called meritorious.

In antiquity, the Left Historiographer recorded actions, and the Right Historiographer recorded words. Good and bad deeds alike were recorded in full. Under the Han, the Diaries of Activity and Repose of the Western Capital were instituted within the imperial court, and those of the Eastern Capital were compiled within the palace. These, too, preserved the intent of antiquity. Subsequently, the Records of Current Government began with Yao Shu, and the Daily Calendar began with Wei Zhiyi. Although their intentions may not have been entirely impartial, their timely recording enabled the events of a dynasty to escape oblivion; their work was certainly not without benefit. We reverently reflect that, when our Sagely Progenitor laid the foundations of the dynasty, he issued an order seeking surviving books as early as the bingwu year of the Zhiyuan era [?]. In the autumn of the guichou year of Hongwu [1373], he again…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
命官以修日曆當是時
大業甫定軍國務殷日不暇給而乃從事乎
此所謂急先務者非耶執事謂可以占
聖謨之弘遠誠哉言矣愚嘗伏讀我
憲宗之續通鑑綱目其載
聖祖諭詹同有曰二帝三王之書不盡傳於今
漢武帝購求遺書六經始出其闡聖賢之學
有功於後世繹斯言也則知其注意於典籍
者至矣於時天祿石渠之藏胠分類别燦
===
然完備何至有散逸之虞又嘗竊觀學士
宋濂之文其序日曆有曰自
上起臨濠以踐天位事蹟莫不具載顧
帝德難名度越前王者不可一二識今之所書
頗得其實而無愧推此意也則其用心於
紀載者悉矣於時金匱石室之編文核事
詳爛焉昭著何至有疎畧之患百七十年
來因成法而紹前休宜其日加盛焉而或
未能盡如其故者何哉雖微執事之問而

命官以修日曆。當是時，大業甫定，軍國務殷，日不暇給，而乃從事乎此，所謂急先務者非耶？執事謂可以占聖謨之弘遠，誠哉言矣！愚嘗伏讀我憲宗之《續通鑑綱目》，其載聖祖諭詹同有曰：「二帝三王之書不盡傳於今，漢武帝購求遺書，六經始出。其闡聖賢之學，有功於後世。」繹斯言也，則知其注意於典籍者至矣。於時，天祿石渠之藏，胠分類别，燦然完備，何至有散逸之虞？

又嘗竊觀學士宋濂之文，其序《日曆》有曰：「自上起臨濠以踐天位，事蹟莫不具載。顧帝德難名，度越前王者，不可一二識。今之所書，頗得其實而無愧。」推此意也，則其用心於紀載者悉矣。於時，金匱石室之編，文核事詳，爛焉昭著，何至有疎畧之患？百七十年來，因成法而紹前休，宜其日加盛焉，而或未能盡如其故者，何哉？雖微執事之問，而
translation_en:
…appointed officials to compile the Daily Calendar. At that time, the great enterprise of founding the dynasty had only just been secured. Military and state affairs were pressing, and each day afforded insufficient time; nevertheless, he undertook this work. Was this not what is meant by giving priority to the most urgent tasks? You say that this reveals the breadth and foresight of his sagely designs: how true your words are! I have reverently read our Emperor Xianzong’s Continuation of the Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror. It records this instruction from Shengzu, our sagely founding emperor, to Zhan Tong: “The writings of the Two Emperors and Three Kings have not all survived to the present. Emperor Wu of the Han purchased and sought out lost books, and only then did the Six Classics emerge. In elucidating the learning of the sages and worthies, he rendered a service to later generations.” Reflecting on these words, we see how complete was his devotion to the classical writings. At that time, the collections of the Tianlu and Shiqu imperial libraries were arranged by category [?], splendidly complete. How could there have been any fear of their dispersal and loss?

I have also read the writings of Academician Song Lian. His preface to the Daily Calendar says: “From His Majesty’s rise at Linhao to his accession to the imperial throne, all his deeds are recorded in full. Yet the emperor’s virtue is difficult to describe: the ways in which he surpasses former kings cannot be recorded merely one or two at a time. What is written here captures the truth fairly well and gives no cause for shame.” Considering the intent of these words, we see how thoroughly he devoted himself to historical recording. At that time, the compilations preserved in metal caskets and stone chambers were accurate in wording and detailed in their accounts of events, brilliantly clear. How could there have been any concern about omissions or inadequacy? Over the past hundred and seventy years, established practices have been followed and earlier achievements carried forward. These undertakings ought to have flourished increasingly with each passing day. Why, then, have some failed fully to match their former condition? Even without your question, …

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
愚也固竊有疑於中矣以藏書言之自祕
書之官既罷凡諸文籍皆歸
內閣而無别儲遺失者不聞有所購求闕畧
者不聞有所修補而司筦籥者未必擅校
讐之能矧
禁署深嚴外臣莫窺則先王之遺訓累世之
珎藏殘逸無統安能免乎往年大臣嘗請
繙校
內閣之書固有見也然愚以為書不可徒校
===
也亦惟典之者得其人而已矣必也極一
時之選以充掌故之職如漢西京之制外
則太史博士內則延閣祕室分别以儲而
奇祕罕傳者復訂正而刋布焉凡成一家
之書無不羅而致之如此則典籍具存有
以為朝夕考求之助庶幾
聖祖之盛心可繼矣以史職言之自記注之銜
既廢所謂史官者徒有具員而無定業
廟堂之謀議絕不與聞

廟堂之謀議絶不與聞
punctuated:
愚也固竊有疑於中矣。以藏書言之，自祕書之官既罷，凡諸文籍皆歸內閣，而無别儲。遺失者不聞有所購求，闕畧者不聞有所修補，而司筦籥者未必擅校讐之能。矧禁署深嚴，外臣莫窺，則先王之遺訓、累世之珎藏，殘逸無統，安能免乎？往年大臣嘗請繙校內閣之書，固有見也。然愚以為書不可徒校也，亦惟典之者得其人而已矣。必也極一時之選，以充掌故之職，如漢西京之制，外則太史博士，內則延閣祕室，分别以儲，而奇祕罕傳者復訂正而刋布焉。凡成一家之書，無不羅而致之。如此，則典籍具存，有以為朝夕考求之助，庶幾聖祖之盛心可繼矣。
以史職言之，自記注之銜既廢，所謂史官者徒有具員，而無定業，廟堂之謀議絕不與聞。
translation_en:
…I, in my ignorance, have indeed privately harbored doubts about this. As for the preservation of books, since the offices responsible for the palace library were abolished, all writings and records have come under the Grand Secretariat, with no separate repository. We hear of no efforts to purchase or seek out lost works, nor of any repairs or supplementation of incomplete ones. Those who hold the keys do not necessarily possess skill in textual collation. Moreover, the palace offices are secluded and strictly guarded, and officials of the outer court cannot inspect them. How, then, can the teachings bequeathed by former kings and the treasured collections accumulated over successive reigns escape damage, loss, and disorder? In past years, high ministers requested that the books of the Grand Secretariat be examined and collated; their proposal certainly showed insight. Yet I believe that books require more than collation: what matters is securing the right people to administer them. The finest men of the age must be selected to fill the posts responsible for historical records and precedents. Following the system of the Western Han, the books should be stored separately: outside the palace, with the Grand Astrologer and the Erudites; inside, in the Yange and the secret repositories. Rare and little-circulated works should also be corrected and printed for distribution. Every work constituting the writings of an individual author or school should be sought out and acquired. In this way, the full collection of canonical works and other writings would be preserved, providing resources for daily consultation and inquiry. We might thereby carry forward the lofty intentions of the sagely founding emperor.
As for the duties of historians, since the title of diarist was abolished, the so-called historiographers have merely filled the allotted posts, without regular duties. They are entirely excluded from hearing the deliberations of the highest councils of state…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
宮省之言動邈不相及而司撰述者惟知據
案牘之文則政事之興革人才之舉錯是
非失實安能免乎往年廷臣嘗請仍設起
居之官非無意也然愚以爲官不必更設
也亦惟居之者盡其職而已矣必也求三
長之士以勝載筆之任如唐貞觀之規進
則立於螭坳退則集於虎觀隨事紀之而
諸司所行者復按日而采錄焉凡載片言
之楮無不斂而藏之如此則史文詳贍可
===
以爲異日筆削之資庶幾
聖祖之初意不失矣抑愚也嘗側聞先達之緒
言而有感焉丘文莊之論曰經籍者聖賢
垂世立教之言載道爲治之具傳之數千
百年以至我使由我而廢墜放失後之人
能不歸咎於今日哉楊文貞之論曰天下
萬世事當以天下萬世之心處之不然無
論巨細皆當獲罪神明是則文莊之心眞
知書之爲重而欲典之者必得其人矣文

宮省之言動邈不相及，而司撰述者惟知據案牘之文，則政事之興革、人才之舉錯，是非失實安能免乎？往年廷臣嘗請仍設起居之官，非無意也。然愚以爲官不必更設也，亦惟居之者盡其職而已矣。必也求三長之士，以勝載筆之任，如唐貞觀之規，進則立於螭坳，退則集於虎觀，隨事紀之，而諸司所行者復按日而采錄焉。凡載片言之楮，無不斂而藏之。如此則史文詳贍，可以爲異日筆削之資，庶幾聖祖之初意不失矣。
抑愚也嘗側聞先達之緒言而有感焉。丘文莊之論曰：「經籍者，聖賢垂世立教之言，載道爲治之具。傳之數千百年以至我，使由我而廢墜放失，後之人能不歸咎於今日哉？」楊文貞之論曰：「天下萬世事，當以天下萬世之心處之。不然，無論巨細，皆當獲罪神明。」是則文莊之心，眞知書之爲重，而欲典之者必得其人矣。文

…The words and actions within the palace remain far beyond their reach, while those charged with compiling history know only to rely on the wording of official documents. How, then, can their accounts of the institution and abolition of policies and the advancement and dismissal of talented men avoid misjudging right and wrong and misrepresenting the facts? In past years, court officials proposed restoring the posts of Imperial Diarists; this was not without purpose. Yet I humbly believe that there is no need to establish additional posts: those who hold office need only fulfill their duties. Men possessing the three strengths of a historian—talent, learning, and judgment—must be sought to undertake the responsibility of wielding the brush. Following the practice of the Tang Zhenguan reign, they should stand beside the dragon-carved recess at the throne steps when attending court and assemble at the Tiger Observatory when they withdraw, recording events as they occur. They should also collect daily records of the actions of the various offices. Every sheet bearing even a few words should be gathered and preserved. In this way, the historical record would be detailed and ample, providing material for future historical compilation and revision. Thus, perhaps, the original intention of the Sagely Progenitor would not be lost.
Furthermore, I have heard something of the teachings left by our eminent predecessors and have been moved by them. Qiu Wenzhuang said: “The classics and other writings contain the words through which sages and worthies established teachings for succeeding ages; they are instruments for conveying the Way and governing. They have been transmitted through hundreds and thousands of years down to us. If through us they fall into neglect and become scattered and lost, can later generations fail to lay the blame upon our own day?” Yang Wenzhen said: “The affairs of all under Heaven and of all ages must be handled with a heart that embraces all under Heaven and all ages. Otherwise, whether the matter is great or small, one will incur guilt before the spirits.” Wenzhuang thus truly understood the importance of books and wished to ensure that suitable men were found to take charge of them. title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
貞之心眞知史之爲重而欲作之者必盡
其職矣故必以二公之心爲心而後可以
舉其事盡其道而無忝也否則欲不爲後
人之所咎神明之所罪得乎狂斐之言如
此幸轉而
聞之於
上或可爲
聖孝繼述萬一之助云
第三問
袁福徵
同考試官教諭陳批經傳之義至深且
賾近世時文之習勝而士之究心者鮮矣子能
剖析詳明不惑衆論而憂深慮遠復爲衞道之
計所謂豪傑之士者非耶
同考試官教諭陳批稽古之學折衷之
論策場似此者絶少錄之以破羣疑
考試官右中允閔批詳說反約確有定論使程
朱復起必以子爲能得其心矣

translation_en:
…Wenzhen’s mind truly recognized the importance of history and wished those who compiled it to fulfill their duties completely. Thus, only by taking the concerns of these two gentlemen as one’s own can one undertake this work and fully carry out its proper principles without disgrace. Otherwise, could one escape the reproach of later generations and condemnation by the spirits? Such are my presumptuous words. I hope they may be conveyed to His Majesty; perhaps they may offer some infinitesimal assistance to his sagely filial devotion in continuing and carrying forward his predecessors’ work.
Third Policy Question
Yuan Fuzheng
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: The meanings of the classics and their commentaries are profoundly deep and intricate. In recent times, the practice of fashionable examination prose has prevailed, and few scholars have applied themselves thoroughly to these meanings. You analyze them clearly and in detail, remaining unconfused by competing opinions. With deep concern and far-reaching thought, you also devise means of defending the Way. Are you not what is called a scholar of outstanding ability?
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: Learning grounded in the investigation of antiquity, arguments that judiciously weigh competing views: work like this is exceedingly rare in the policy-essay examination. I select it for inclusion to dispel the many doubts.
Comment by Examiner Min, Right Mentor: Through detailed exposition, you return to the essentials and arrive firmly at definite conclusions. Were Cheng and Zhu to rise again, they would surely judge you capable of grasping their intentions.

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官侍讀華批揚確衆論悉中肯綮是究
心理學者錄之
釋經者取其言之有契於道而不惟其人
與人者取其學之可進於道而不惟其世
夫道之在人心古今一而已矣是故或著
論於道學未明之先與大儒之說不相謀
而自相合者取之可也或著論於道學既
明之後與大儒之說若相反而寔相成者
取之亦可也君子惟求其是而已矣而何
===
人與世之可拘哉嘅自孔子沒而微言絕
七十子喪而大義乖百家殊方指意不同
經傳之微詞奧義或幾乎隱矣至宋程朱
大儒出而始闡明之其有功於吾道夫人
而知之也然天下之理有開必先而造道
之言無往不合是故先程朱而出者如表
中庸以明道統之傳可謂知道矣然仕蕭

指清心以為出治之本可謂識治矣然相

Comment by Examiner Hua, Reader-in-Waiting: He critically examines the various arguments [?], consistently getting to the heart of the matter. This is someone who has devoted his mind to the Learning of Principle. Select this essay.

In interpreting the Classics, one should accept statements that accord with the Way, without judging solely by who made them; in approving a person, one should consider whether his learning can advance toward the Way, without judging solely by the age in which he lived. The Way within the human mind has always been the same, in antiquity and today. Thus, writings composed before the Learning of the Way had been clarified may agree spontaneously with the teachings of the great Confucian masters, without their authors having consulted one another: these may be accepted. Writings composed after the Learning of the Way had been clarified may seem to contradict the teachings of the great masters while actually complementing them: these too may be accepted. The gentleman seeks only what is right. How could he be constrained by the person or the age?

Alas, after Confucius died, his subtle teachings ceased to be transmitted; after the seventy disciples passed away, the great principles became distorted. The hundred schools pursued divergent paths and differed in their intentions, so that the subtle expressions and profound meanings of the Classics and their commentaries almost fell into obscurity. Only when the great Confucian masters Cheng and Zhu emerged in the Song were these elucidated. Everyone knows the service they rendered to our Way. Yet whenever the principles of the world are disclosed, there must be precursors; and statements that attain the Way agree wherever they are found. Thus, among those who preceded Cheng and Zhu, someone who brought the Doctrine of the Mean to prominence to illuminate the transmission of the succession of the Way may be said to have understood the Way. Yet among those who served the Xiao Liang dynasty and expounded its meaning at the Shilin Hall was He Chen. title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
宇文周而著其義於六條之書者則有如
蘇綽敬之一言百聖心法也而徐幹已詳
論於法象之篇權之一字千載絕學也而
陸贄已極論於易鎭之疏性情義利之辨
漢詔嘗勅東平傅相矣而君子謂此等語
有所自來優柔厭飫之語杜預嘗序左氏
春秋矣而君子謂循其言可以入道至於
專經之家若劉歆圖書經緯之言孔穎達
陰陽九六之義鄭玄五聲六律十二管還
===
相為宫之說皆卓然有可稱述者是豈無
所本乎蓋其去古未遠淵源所自或有得
於聖門之緒論耳鄉使數君子生於程朱
之時而相與講明乎正學則反博歸約其
所成就寧止是耶後程朱而出者如論大
學格致之傳本無所闕知止知至之文即
其錯簡董矩堂車清臣之說也論周禮冬
官之文初未嘗亡五官各屬之中其實錯
見俞庭椿王次點之說也謂詩之二南相

punctuated:
宇文周而著其義於六條之書者，則有如蘇綽。敬之一言，百聖心法也，而徐幹已詳論於法象之篇；權之一字，千載絕學也，而陸贄已極論於易鎭之疏。性情義利之辨，漢詔嘗勅東平傅相矣，而君子謂此等語有所自來；優柔厭飫之語，杜預嘗序左氏春秋矣，而君子謂循其言可以入道。至於專經之家，若劉歆圖書經緯之言、孔穎達陰陽九六之義、鄭玄五聲六律十二管還相為宫之說，皆卓然有可稱述者，是豈無所本乎？蓋其去古未遠，淵源所自，或有得於聖門之緒論耳。鄉使數君子生於程朱之時，而相與講明乎正學，則反博歸約，其所成就寧止是耶？

後程朱而出者，如論《大學》格致之傳本無所闕，知止知至之文即其錯簡，董矩堂、車清臣之說也；論《周禮》冬官之文初未嘗亡，五官各屬之中，其實錯見，俞庭椿、王次點之說也；謂《詩》之二南相
translation_en:
… under the Yuwen Zhou and set forth these principles in a document of Six Articles: Su Chuo was such a man. Reverence is the method of cultivating the mind shared by all sages, yet Xu Gan had already discussed it fully in his chapter “Models and Images.” Judicious weighing of circumstances is a learning whose transmission had been broken for a thousand years, yet Lu Zhi had already discussed it exhaustively in his memorial on changing military commands. A Han imperial edict once instructed the Grand Tutor and Chancellor of Dongping on the distinctions between human nature and the feelings, and between righteousness and profit; learned gentlemen have observed that such statements had an antecedent source. Du Yu had already spoken of leisurely immersion and thorough assimilation in his preface to Zuo’s Spring and Autumn Annals; learned gentlemen have said that following his words could lead one into the Way. As for specialists in individual classics, there are Liu Xin’s statements about the warp and weft of the Chart and the Writing, Kong Yingda’s explanation of yin and yang and the numbers nine and six, and Zheng Xuan’s account of the five notes, six pitch standards, and twelve pitch pipes taking turns to serve as the gong, or tonic. All contain outstanding points worthy of commendation and exposition. Could these possibly have lacked a foundation? These men were not far removed from antiquity, and the sources of their learning may have preserved something of the teachings handed down from the sage’s school. Had these gentlemen lived in the time of Cheng and Zhu and joined them in elucidating orthodox learning, they could have returned from broad learning to its essential principles. Would their achievements then have stopped at this?

Among those who came after Cheng and Zhu, Dong Jutang and Che Qingchen argued that the commentary on investigating things and extending knowledge in the Great Learning originally lacked nothing, and that the passages on knowing where to rest and on knowledge reaching its utmost were its misplaced slips. Yu Tingchun and Wang Cidian argued that the text concerning the Winter Offices in the Rites of Zhou had never been lost, but was actually interspersed among the subordinate offices of the other five divisions. There is also the claim that the two Nan sections of the Book of Odes correspond to one another …

配各十一篇甘棠何彼穠矣野有死麕三
詩皆他篇之誤入此論出於王魯齋也而
所著讀易記諸書尤多發明謂易之諸卦
各有文言而亡之今大傳中釋卦爻之辭
皆其散逸而僅存此論出於熊朋來也而
所著五經說一編亦多辨正日抄著於黃
東發論天地定位一章必非先天之卦位
而疑邵子之圖未可盡從通考作於馬端
臨論鄭衛諸詩必非淫者所自作而疑小
===
序之說難以盡廢至於
本朝諸名公若楊文懿之私抄王端毅之意
見程學士之詩考皆確然有以自信者是
豈無所見乎蓋其反求諸心有所未安而
不苟同於先儒之成說耳鄉使數君子游
程朱之門而相與上下其議論則去短集
長其所造詣詎可量耶大抵斯理之在人
心未嘗不同惟其學之所造有深淺故其
論之所及有偏全耳且程朱之解經固未

This argument originated with Wang Luzhai. His Notes on Reading the Changes (Du Yi ji) and other writings contain especially numerous illuminating insights. The contention that each hexagram of the Changes originally had a Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan), subsequently lost, and that the explanations of hexagram and line statements now found in the Great Commentary are merely the surviving remnants of those dispersed texts originated with Xiong Penglai. His Explanations of the Five Classics (Wujing shuo) likewise contains many clarifications and corrections. Huang Dongfa wrote the Daily Notes (Richao), arguing that the passage beginning “Heaven and earth take their positions” certainly did not describe the hexagram positions of the Before Heaven arrangement, and questioning whether Master Shao’s diagram could be followed in every respect. Ma Duanlin wrote the Comprehensive Examination (Tongkao), arguing that the poems of Zheng and Wei certainly were not composed by the licentious people themselves, and questioning whether the explanations in the Minor Prefaces could be wholly discarded. As for the distinguished gentlemen of our own dynasty, works such as Yang Wenyi’s Private Notes (Sichao), Wang Duanyi’s Opinions (Yijian), and Academician Cheng’s Examination of the Odes (Shikao) all express firmly grounded convictions. Could these men have lacked insight? They simply searched their own hearts, found points with which they were not at ease, and would not casually assent to the established explanations of earlier Confucian scholars. Had these gentlemen studied under Cheng and Zhu and together thoroughly debated their interpretations, eliminating shortcomings and bringing together strengths, how could their attainments have been measured? In general, this principle as present in human hearts has never differed; it is only because people attain different depths in learning that their discussions are partial or comprehensive. title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
嘗盡廢前人之說藉令其聞後儒之論而
有當於心寧不欣然取之也彼譁而攻之
直流俗之見耳惡足以知大賢君子至公
無我之心哉今
國家以經術造士濂洛關閩之書夫人習焉
而所謂古註疏者特視為長物而猥以不
誦絕之此有志於存古者所為太息也盍
思所以表章之乎夫近世二三君子願為
程朱之忠臣如執事所稱者其所辨論不
===
===
過文義之間小小出入而已至其大體則
詎容或議而可輕訾之乎今世乃有肆然
以道學自任欲蔑棄程朱之傳註而盡用
其私說天下之學者厭常喜新方靡然從
之末流之弊殆未知其底止矣愚也重為
吾道憂之孟子曰能言距楊墨者聖人之
徒也韓昌黎曰障百川而東之迴狂瀾於
既倒竊於執事有望焉
第四問

思所以表章之乎夫近世二三君子願爲

===
過文義之間小小出入而已至其大體則
詎容或議而可輕訾之乎今世乃有肆然
以道學自任欲蔑棄程朱之傳註而盡用
其私說天下之學者厭常喜新方靡然從
之末流之弊殆未知其底止矣愚也重爲
吾道憂之孟子曰能言距楊墨者聖人之
徒也韓昌黎曰障百川而東之迴狂瀾於
既倒竊於執事有望焉
第四問
punctuated:
嘗盡廢前人之說。藉令其聞後儒之論而有當於心，寧不欣然取之也？彼譁而攻之，直流俗之見耳，惡足以知大賢君子至公無我之心哉！今國家以經術造士，濂洛關閩之書，夫人習焉，而所謂古註疏者，特視為長物，而猥以不誦絕之，此有志於存古者所為太息也。盍思所以表章之乎？夫近世二三君子，願為程朱之忠臣，如執事所稱者，其所辨論，不過文義之間小小出入而已。至其大體，則詎容或議，而可輕訾之乎？今世乃有肆然以道學自任，欲蔑棄程朱之傳註而盡用其私說。天下之學者厭常喜新，方靡然從之，末流之弊，殆未知其底止矣。愚也重為吾道憂之。孟子曰：「能言距楊墨者，聖人之徒也。」韓昌黎曰：「障百川而東之，迴狂瀾於既倒。」竊於執事有望焉。

第四問
translation_en:
…ever wholly discarded the explanations of earlier scholars. Suppose they heard the arguments of later scholars and found them consonant with their own understanding: would they not gladly adopt them? Those who noisily attack them merely express commonplace opinions. How could they comprehend the supremely impartial and selfless hearts of great worthies and exemplary men?

Today the state forms its scholars through the study of the Classics. Everyone studies the writings of the Lian, Luo, Guan, and Min traditions, yet the ancient commentaries and subcommentaries are treated merely as superfluous things, summarily excluded as texts not to be studied. This is what makes those committed to preserving antiquity sigh deeply. Why not consider how to bring these works to prominence? As for those few gentlemen of recent times who wish to be loyal servants of Cheng and Zhu, such as those you have mentioned, their debates concern only minor differences in the interpretation of words and passages. As to the main substance of their teaching, how could it admit of objection, and how could one lightly disparage it?

Yet today there are those who presumptuously claim responsibility for the Learning of the Way, wishing to cast aside the commentaries of Cheng and Zhu and rely entirely on their own private interpretations. Scholars throughout the realm, weary of the familiar and delighted by novelty, are now flocking to follow them. There is scarcely any knowing where the abuses resulting from this trend will end. I, in my ignorance, am all the more anxious for our Way. Mengzi said: “Those able to argue against Yang and Mo are followers of the sages.” Han Changli said: “Dam the hundred rivers and turn them eastward; turn back the raging flood after it has broken loose.” I venture to place my hopes in you.

Fourth Question

You alone enumerate the points without omission. Could anyone deny that you are a man of extensive learning? You truly deserve first place.”

Comment by Examiner Hua, Reader-in-Waiting: “All five policy essays are detailed and ample, but this one is even better. It is included here as representative of the others.”

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
唐書宋史之必假於更正不容已也請因
明問而陳之紀傳書志之體前世未有也
其肇於司馬遷乎遷之史起於軒轅迄於
漢武採摭經傳馳騁古今上下數千載固
非一代之史也至於班固乃遵其軌轍加
之檃括究西都之終始窮劉氏之廢興苞
舉一代以國名書而其制遂定後之作者
遞相沿襲莫能改焉然而世異風移質文
互變人品高下著作亦殊故操觚藝苑雖
===
非一家而追蹤史漢卒未多得良有以也
今自唐書言之唐之設兵近古而制屢變
更其末也則壞而為禁軍此亂之所由也
可以弗志乎藩鎮專地而力相併吞其甚
也則起而弱王室此變之最大者可以無
表乎悉心奉國如長孫無忌當代之功臣
也顧與奸諛之敬宗並書起衰濟溺如韓
退之振古之豪傑也顧與浮誕之禹錫同
傳以文苑目劉蕡是畧其鯁直之操以外

《唐書》《宋史》之必假於更正，不容已也。請因明問而陳之。紀傳書志之體，前世未有也，其肇於司馬遷乎？遷之史，起於軒轅，迄於漢武，採摭經傳，馳騁古今，上下數千載，固非一代之史也。至於班固，乃遵其軌轍，加之檃括，究西都之終始，窮劉氏之廢興，苞舉一代，以國名書，而其制遂定。後之作者，遞相沿襲，莫能改焉。然而世異風移，質文互變，人品高下，著作亦殊。故操觚藝苑，雖非一家，而追蹤《史》《漢》，卒未多得，良有以也。
今自《唐書》言之，唐之設兵近古，而制屢變更，其末也則壞而為禁軍，此亂之所由也，可以弗志乎？藩鎮專地，而力相併吞，其甚也則起而弱王室，此變之最大者，可以無表乎？悉心奉國，如長孫無忌，當代之功臣也，顧與奸諛之敬宗並書；起衰濟溺，如韓退之，振古之豪傑也，顧與浮誕之禹錫同傳。以文苑目劉蕡，是畧其鯁直之操；以外
translation_en:
…the History of the Tang and the History of the Song must undergo correction; this cannot be left undone. Allow me to explain in response to your discerning question. The format of basic annals, biographies, and treatises had not existed in earlier ages: did it not originate with Sima Qian? His history began with Xuanyuan and extended down to Emperor Wu of the Han. Drawing material from the classics and their commentaries, it ranged freely through ancient and recent times, spanning several thousand years. It was certainly no history of a single dynasty. Ban Gu then followed his precedent, refining its organization, thoroughly examining the Western Han from beginning to end and tracing the decline and rise of the Liu house. He encompassed a single dynasty and named his book after it; thus the format became established. Subsequent writers followed one another in adopting it, and none could alter it. Yet as ages differed and customs shifted, simplicity and refinement alternated; authors differed in personal caliber, and their writings likewise varied. Thus, although many writers wielded their brushes in the literary world, few ultimately succeeded in following in the footsteps of the Records of the Historian and the History of the Han. There are sound reasons for this.
Let us begin with the History of the Tang. The Tang military establishment approximated that of antiquity, but its institutions underwent repeated changes. In the end they deteriorated into the palace armies: this was a source of disorder. Could it be left without a treatise? Regional military commands monopolized territory and forcibly annexed one another. At their worst, they rose up and weakened the imperial house. This was the greatest of the upheavals: could it be left without chronological tables? A man such as Zhangsun Wuji devoted himself wholeheartedly to serving the state and was a meritorious minister of his age, yet he is recorded alongside the treacherous flatterer Jingzong. A man such as Han Tuizhi revived what was declining and rescued what was drowning—a hero outstanding through the ages—yet he shares a biographical chapter with the frivolous and fanciful Yuxi. To classify Liu Fen under “Men of Letters” is to slight his integrity and forthrightness; to classify someone under “Imperial Relatives”…

translation_en:
…to classify Wu Shu [?] among imperial relatives seems to obscure his exceptional conduct. These are among its more conspicuous faults. Its other inconsistencies and omissions, which make it unsuitable as a model, cannot readily be enumerated in full. Zeng Gongliang said: “Its arrangement lacks method; its fullness and brevity are ill proportioned; its literary qualities are undistinguished; and its factual accounts are fragmentary.” This is indeed a sound judgment. Why was this so? The book was compiled under the Shi family's Jin dynasty, and its compiler was Liu Xu. Warfare raged, and usurpations and rebellions followed one another: literary culture had fallen into profound decline. Liu Xu himself served two dynasties and transgressed the bounds of ritual propriety and righteousness. How could one demand impartiality from him in assigning praise and blame?
The founding emperor of the Song established the dynasty, honored literary learning, and exalted the Way. By the Qingli and Jiayou reign periods, talented men appeared in succession, and writing was refined and correct. Emperor Renzong therefore ordered Ouyang Xiu and Song Qi jointly to examine the old text, rectify its principles and conventions, gather scattered and lost materials, and polish its grand prose. They completed four additional treatises, compiled four tables, removed sixty-one biographies, and added three hundred and thirty-one. Only then were the enlightened rulers and eminent ministers of the Tang's three hundred years, its state institutions and court regulations, the varieties of popular customs and official affairs, and the causes of security and danger, order and disorder, all clearly set forth for readers to examine. As the saying goes, “Its factual content exceeds that of its predecessor, while its wording is more concise than the old text.” This is a large claim, but no exaggeration. Once the new history appeared, it was esteemed and trusted throughout the realm; the old history consequently fell out of use, and people no longer read it. Ah! How could the achievement of Ouyang Xiu and Song Qi be considered slight? As for the Song …

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
史言之其本紀所以述天子之大經大法
也而乃委曲泛濫兼收細行甚或下及於
臣事列傳所以錄臣子之嘉謨嘉猷也而
乃綴緝叢委誇詡爵寵遂使猥同於家乘
紀典禮而拜俯之臚贊屢書載儀衛而名
物之瑣細迭見道學儒林一途也而別為
兩目未必人物之皆當忠孝隱逸殊行也
而採及百人未必名實之相符此皆其失
之尤大者若其間煩章冗句不知所裁又
===
未易徧舉也阿魯圖之言有曰先理致而
後文詞崇道德而黜功利書法以之而矜
式彞倫賴是而匡扶殆虛語耳此其故何
也蓋是史之作其時則胡元也其人則脫
脫也夷狄為王風俗大壞文氣之衰久矣
而脫脫位居元宰政事之才雖其優裕安
能兼彼文史之任乎洪惟我
國家敷揚道化經緯人文不特表章六經而
已綱目有續編通鑑有纂要胡元有全史

阿魯圖之言有曰：「先理致而後文詞，崇道德而黜功利，書法以之而矜式，彞倫賴是而匡扶。」殆虛語耳。此其故何也？蓋是史之作，其時則胡元也，其人則脫脫也。夷狄為王，風俗大壞，文氣之衰久矣。而脫脫位居元宰，政事之才雖其優裕，安能兼彼文史之任乎？
洪惟我國家敷揚道化，經緯人文，不特表章六經而已。《綱目》有續編，《通鑑》有纂要，胡元有全史。
translation_en:
…As for the History of the Song, its Basic Annals should recount the sovereign’s great principles and fundamental institutions. Yet they wander into excessive detail, indiscriminately including minor conduct and even descending to the affairs of ministers. Its Biographies should record the fine plans and counsels of subjects. Yet they pile together collected materials and boast of titles and imperial favor, reducing themselves to the level of family chronicles. In recording ceremonial institutions, they repeatedly set down the ceremonial calls directing bows and prostrations; in describing ceremonial guards, they continually present trivial details of names and objects. Learning of the Way and the Forest of Scholars belong to a single path, yet they are separated into two categories, and the persons assigned to them are not necessarily all appropriately placed. Loyalty and filial piety, reclusion and withdrawal, represent distinct forms of conduct; yet the selection extends to a hundred persons whose reputations do not necessarily accord with reality. These are among its most serious faults. As for its tedious passages and redundant sentences, left unpruned, these too are difficult to enumerate fully.
Alutu once said: “Give precedence to principle and meaning over literary expression; exalt the Way and moral virtue, and reject achievement and profit. Thereby the methods of historical writing acquire an exemplary standard, and the enduring human relationships receive support and correction.” These are probably no more than empty words. Why is this so? This history was compiled in the time of the barbarian Yuan, and the man responsible was Tuotuo. With barbarians ruling as kings, customs had fallen into utter decay, and literary vitality had long been declining. Although Tuotuo, occupying the position of chief councilor, possessed ample talent for government affairs, how could he also undertake responsibility for literature and history?
We reverently reflect that our dynasty spreads the transforming influence of the Way and brings order to human culture. It has done more than merely give prominence to the Six Classics. The Outline and Details (Gangmu) has a continuation; the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian) has a compiled digest; and the barbarian Yuan has a complete history…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
述作咸備文章煥焉而獨於宋史未及刋
正是誠有待於
今日者也我
皇上萬幾之暇慨然念此
面諭輔臣亟加修纂天下綴文之士拭目以
俟其成久矣愚何人斯而能贊一辭哉竊
惟自古作史者莫良於遷固然史記敘三
千年事五十萬言漢書敘二百四十年事
八十萬言而張輔著論優遷劣固則作史
之煩省得失可知矣明問所謂刪繁舉要
者豈非今日之要務哉然其詳其簡各有
法焉非徒嚴於裁削而後謂之簡工於纂
組而後謂之詳也觀班固之稱史記曰辨
而不華質而不俚范曄之稱漢書曰贍而
不穢詳而有體則史法之在遷固者可知
也等而上之孔子嘗刪書矣嘗修春秋矣
而孔安國稱之曰芟夷煩亂翦截浮辭舉
其宏綱撮其機要則刪繁舉要之指不但

translation_en:
…Historical writings are fully provided, and literary accomplishment shines forth; yet the History of the Song alone has not been revised and corrected. This is indeed a task that has awaited the present day. Amid the myriad affairs of state, our Emperor has found time to reflect earnestly upon this matter and personally instructed his chief ministers to undertake its revision and compilation without delay. Men of letters throughout the realm have long awaited its completion with eager eyes. Who am I, in my ignorance, to contribute even a word?

I humbly consider that, among historians since antiquity, none has surpassed Sima Qian and Ban Gu. Yet the Records of the Grand Historian recounts three thousand years of events in five hundred thousand words, whereas the History of the Han recounts two hundred and forty years in eight hundred thousand words. Zhang Fu wrote a discourse ranking Sima Qian above Ban Gu: from this one may discern the merits and failings of prolixity and concision in historical writing. Is not what your illuminating question calls “cutting the superfluous and presenting the essentials” precisely an urgent task of the present day? Yet fullness and brevity each have their proper principles. Brevity does not consist merely in stringent cutting, nor fullness merely in skillful literary weaving.

Consider Ban Gu’s praise of the Records of the Grand Historian: “Discriminating without being ornate, plain without being vulgar”; and Fan Ye’s praise of the History of the Han: “Ample without being cluttered, detailed yet properly structured.” From these judgments one may understand the principles of historical writing embodied by Sima Qian and Ban Gu. Ascending to a still higher level, Confucius once edited the Documents and revised the Spring and Autumn Annals. Kong Anguo praised him in these words: “He weeded out the excessive and confused, cut away empty phrases, set forth the broad framework, and gathered the essential points.” Thus, the purport of cutting the superfluous and presenting the essentials is not merely…

title: 嘉靖二十二年應天府鄉試錄
text:
合遷固之法而已蓋與孔子之道相符契
焉歐宋又何足言耶矧今名卿鉅儒良史
直筆充衍館閣超邁漢唐誠取宋史而修
之則一揮翰之間蕪穢洗而華藻生義意
周而篇章約可以新一代之書備
九重之覽矣雖然愚復有說焉賢如歐宋其
立例修辭可謂審矣然削去詔令使一代
王言之無徵好用奇字使後世讀者之易
厭故劉元城謂事增文省正為新書之病
===
===
而司馬温公作通鑑獨於舊書有取焉吁
二公尚然可弗慎歟故愚以為今日
上之任夫人也貴行乎四事而下之任其職也
貴稽乎五志而参以三科何謂四事曰重
委任不以他務亂其心思也曰假歲月不
以速成致其率畧也曰專職業雖有選擢
不令輒去也曰訪遺書凡有著述無不搜
羅也舉是以課史職則意嚮篤而在上之
道盡矣何謂五志曰達道義曰彰法戒曰
